The first biostatistician's argument has merit for confirmatory regulatory settings but is stated as an absolute principle, which is too strong: informative priors are valid in many Bayesian adaptive designs. Option D incorrectly equates 'coherent' with 'robust to prior choice' — Bayesian posteriors are coherent given any fixed prior, but choosing among priors is a separate methodological question.
hints: When two reasonable analysts disagree about the prior, and the stopping decision may change depending on which prior is used, what is the most rigorous way to resolve the disagreement?
Bayesian analysis is coherent given a fixed prior — but that coherence does not answer the question of whether the prior itself is the right one to use.

title: Bayesian Bandit: Contextual Arms and Prior Misspecification
scenario_context: A news platform deploys a contextual bandit to personalize article recommendations. The bandit uses a Thompson sampling policy with a ridge regression model for expected click-through rate, conditioned on user features (age bucket, device, reading history length). The bandit is initialized with a prior that assumes all user segments have equal expected CTR across arms. After 2 weeks, engagement analysts notice the bandit performs well for mobile users but poorly for desktop users — desktop CTR has declined 8% since deployment versus baseline. They suspect the prior is misspecified for desktop users. A data scientist proposes three interventions: (1) re-initialize the desktop user segment with a new prior fit from pre-bandit desktop data, (2) add desktop-specific features to the ridge regression, and (3) run a separate bandit for desktop users.
description: Rank the interventions from most to least effective at addressing the core problem.
options: 3, 2, 1 — A separate desktop bandit is best because it eliminates the shared parameter problem; adding features is second because it gives the model more signal; prior re-initialization is least effective because the model will simply re-learn the same incorrect patterns

2, 1, 3 — Adding contextual features is best because it allows the single model to learn desktop-specific patterns; prior re-initialization is second because it gives the desktop segment a better starting point; a separate bandit is least effective because it discards cross-segment information

1, 3, 2 — Prior re-initialization is best because it directly addresses the misspecification; a separate bandit is second because it allows clean learning; adding features is least effective because more features increase variance without fixing the prior

2, 3, 1 — Adding contextual features is best because it most directly addresses the root cause (the model lacks desktop-specific signal); a separate bandit is second because it avoids cross-segment contamination; prior re-initialization is least effective because it is a temporary fix that does not change the model's ability to learn desktop patterns
explanation: The core problem is that the bandit model lacks sufficient desktop-specific signal to learn appropriate arm preferences for that segment. A uniform prior and a model that does not adequately distinguish desktop behavior from mobile behavior will systematically underperform for any segment that behaves differently from the population average. Adding contextual features (intervention 2) most directly addresses this root cause: if the ridge regression model can learn that desktop users respond differently to content types or presentation formats, it will adapt its arm preferences for desktop users as data accumulates. This is the most scalable and enduring fix because it improves the model's representational capacity. A separate bandit (intervention 3) ranks second: it eliminates cross-segment contamination entirely and lets the desktop bandit develop its own arm distribution from scratch. It is not the best option because it discards any generalizable cross-segment signal and introduces operational overhead, but it does address the misspecification more durably than a prior fix alone. Prior re-initialization (intervention 1) is the least durable: it gives the desktop segment a better starting point, but the same ridge regression structure that failed to learn desktop patterns will continue to do so — prior re-initialization does not change the model's ability to represent desktop-specific behavior, so it only delays rather than resolves the problem. Option A ranks a separate bandit above feature addition, undervaluing the model's ability to learn cross-segment patterns when given the right features. Option B places prior re-initialization second over a separate bandit — this is wrong because a better prior does not fix a model that cannot represent the segment; a separate bandit at least learns the right distribution from scratch, making it a more durable second choice.
hints: When a model performs poorly on a specific subgroup, consider whether the issue is in how the model is initialized (prior) or in whether the model architecture can represent the subgroup's behavior at all.
Rank interventions by whether they fix the root cause (model expressiveness), address a symptom temporarily (prior), or avoid the problem by isolation (separate model).

title: Multi-Armed Bandit vs Fixed A/B: Long Horizon Decision
scenario_context: A subscription SaaS company is testing three pricing page variants (A, B, C) against a control. The experiment will run for 8 weeks across 40,000 new visitors per week. Historical data shows pricing experiments at this company have a high variance in outcomes — some variants have large positive effects (>10%), others are neutral or slightly negative. The head of growth wants to use a Thompson sampling bandit to minimize revenue lost during the experiment. The head of analytics argues that for this particular scenario, a fixed 4-arm A/B test with equal allocation is preferable.
description: What is the strongest argument supporting the analytics head's position?
options: A bandit cannot handle 4 arms; Thompson sampling is only valid for binary (2-arm) experiments, making the fixed A/B test the only valid design
The fixed A/B test produces a cleaner causal estimate with well-calibrated confidence intervals, which are required for the post-experiment business review

With high variance in historical outcomes, the bandit may concentrate traffic on a variant that happens to perform well early due to noise rather than true superiority, especially with 40,000 visitors per week and 8 weeks of data — the fixed design ensures the exploration phase is long enough to overcome early noise and identify the true winner more reliably
Fixed A/B tests always provide higher statistical power than bandits for the same total sample size, making the analytics head's position universally correct
explanation: The analytics head's strongest argument is about noise-driven early allocation in a high-variance environment. Thompson sampling concentrates traffic toward the arm with the highest posterior probability of being best. In a high-variance outcome environment, early observations can be noisy — a variant that happens to perform well in the first week due to random fluctuation will accumulate more traffic, reinforcing its dominance in the posterior even if the true effect is no better than control. With 40,000 visitors per week, there is substantial weekly traffic, but 8 weeks is a relatively short window to overcome high-variance outcomes through posterior updating alone. A fixed equal-allocation A/B test forces continued exploration of all arms throughout the experiment, ensuring each arm accumulates enough observations to average out noise before a final decision. The analytics head is also correct that the bandit's regret-reduction advantage is greatest when the true winner has a substantially larger effect and can be identified quickly — which the high-variance historical pattern suggests may not be reliably the case here. Option A is false — Thompson sampling handles multiple arms natively. Option B is a secondary consideration about decision process, not a statistical argument. Option D is false — bandits can have higher or lower power depending on the scenario; 'always higher' is incorrect.
hints: An adaptive allocation method shifts traffic toward the arm that looks best early. In a high-variance environment, what does 'looking best early' actually tell you about true long-term superiority?
Think about the conditions under which a bandit's regret advantage over fixed allocation is largest — and whether those conditions are present when historical effect sizes are highly variable.

title: SUTVA Violation: Social Network Cascade
scenario_context: A social network runs an experiment on a new 'group post reaction' feature — users in the treatment group can react to group posts with an expanded set of emoji. The experiment randomizes 20% of users into treatment. After 4 weeks, the treatment group shows 15% higher group post engagement. However, a network analyst points out that group posts are viewed by all members of a group regardless of their experimental assignment. A treatment user's reaction (using an expanded emoji) is visible to control users in the same group, potentially stimulating their engagement as well. After adjusting for this interference via a network-aware model, the estimated effect drops to 9%. An engineer proposes a simple fix: randomize groups rather than individual users. A scientist pushes back on this proposal.
description: What is the scientist's strongest objection?
options: Group-level randomization is technically infeasible on large social networks because groups have millions of members and cannot be cleanly partitioned

Group-level randomization would eliminate the interference problem but dramatically increases the variance of the treatment effect estimate: groups are highly heterogeneous in size, activity, and user composition, so group-level random assignment introduces much higher variance in the measured treatment and control outcomes compared to individual randomization

Group-level randomization introduces a new problem: users belong to multiple groups, so a user could be in a treatment group for one community and a control group for another, making the individual-level treatment condition ambiguous and reintroducing interference
Group-level randomization is only valid when groups are of equal size; unequal group sizes require a different clustering approach
explanation: The scientist's strongest objection is that group-level randomization does not solve the interference problem if users belong to multiple groups — which is the typical structure on social platforms. A user who is in a treatment group (where expanded emoji reactions are available) will also be a member of control groups (where the feature is unavailable). When that user reacts to a post in their treatment group with an expanded emoji, other control-group users who are also in that same treatment group see it. Conversely, the treatment user sees only standard reactions in their control groups. The user-level treatment condition becomes undefined, and interference across group boundaries persists. Additionally, the treatment user's behavior in control groups is contaminated by their experience in treatment groups. Option A is empirically untrue — many platforms randomize at the group or community level. Option B is a real concern (higher variance with group randomization due to heterogeneous group sizes), but it is a statistical efficiency tradeoff, not a fundamental validity objection. Option D is incorrect — unequal cluster sizes in cluster-randomized experiments are handled via appropriate analysis weights; they do not invalidate the design.
hints: When users belong to multiple groups, and randomization assigns groups (not users) to treatment conditions, what happens to an individual user who is simultaneously in a treatment group and a control group?
Think about whether the proposed solution actually eliminates the interference channel or whether it moves the problem to a different boundary.

title: Network Interference: Bipartite Graph Randomization
scenario_context: An online tutoring marketplace runs an experiment to test an AI-powered question hint system for tutors. Tutors use the system to generate hints for students. The platform has 5,000 tutors and 50,000 students; each student works with 1–3 tutors. The team randomizes tutors into treatment (hint system available) and control (no hint system). After 6 weeks, treatment tutors' students show 8% higher assessment scores. A researcher argues that the estimate is still biased by interference. Some students work with both a treatment tutor and a control tutor: insights a student gains from a treatment tutor's hints may improve their performance with their control tutor as well. The interference flows through students, not directly between tutors. This is described as 'bipartite graph interference.'
description: What is the correct direction of bias in the tutor-level treatment effect estimate?
options: The estimate is biased upward: treatment tutors get credit for score improvements that are partly caused by their students' learning gains from other treatment tutors, inflating the apparent effectiveness of the hint system

The estimate is biased downward: students shared between treatment and control tutors carry learning spillovers from treatment tutors into their sessions with control tutors, raising control tutor student scores and compressing the treatment-control gap

The estimate is unbiased: bipartite graph interference only affects student-level randomization, not tutor-level randomization, because the interference flows through students who are not the unit of randomization

The estimate could be biased in either direction depending on whether treatment tutor spillovers dominate or control group contamination dominates; the direction cannot be determined without knowing the fraction of students who are shared
explanation: The bias is downward, and the direction can be reasoned precisely. Students who work with both a treatment tutor and a control tutor benefit from the hint system (via their treatment tutor) and carry that learning into sessions with their control tutor. The control tutor's student scores are therefore elevated — not by the hint system applied by the control tutor, but by the treatment spillover through the shared student. This elevates the control group's outcome metric, compressing the gap between treatment and control. The treatment effect estimate (treatment tutor student scores minus control tutor student scores) is therefore smaller than the true effect. Option A describes the opposite direction: credit flowing to treatment tutors from other treatment tutors is not the described mechanism; the mechanism is student-mediated spillover into the control arm. Option C is incorrect: bipartite interference affects any randomization where the interference pathway runs through shared units (students in this case) — tutor-level randomization does not eliminate this. Option D correctly notes that the fraction of shared students matters for the magnitude, but the direction of bias (downward) is deterministic given the described mechanism.
hints: Think about what happens to the control group's outcome when some control-group subjects have also been exposed to the treatment through a different connection — does that raise or lower the control group average?
When spillovers from the treatment arm contaminate the control arm's outcomes, does that make the treatment-control gap look bigger or smaller than the true effect?

title: Long-Term Holdout: Novelty Decay vs True Effect
scenario_context: A consumer app launches a major redesign affecting the home screen. A 4% holdout group (600,000 users) is kept on the old design for 12 months to measure long-term effects. At 30 days, treated users show 18% higher daily active use. At 90 days, the gap is 11%. At 180 days, the gap is 7%. At 360 days, the gap is 4%. The product team interprets this as novelty decay: early excitement with the new design fades over time. A researcher challenges this interpretation, offering an alternative explanation.
description: What is the most credible alternative explanation for the declining gap, and what data would distinguish between the two interpretations?
options: The alternative explanation is that control (holdout) users have been learning about the new design from treatment users via social communication, and are partially adapting their habits to the new design despite not having access to it; the distinguishing data would be social graph adjacency between holdout and treatment users

The alternative explanation is that the old design's performance is degrading over 12 months as the product team focuses engineering resources on improving the new design, raising the control group's defect rate and suppressing their engagement; the distinguishing data would be server-side error rates and load times for the control (old design) code path

The alternative explanation is that the holdout group is self-selecting into lower engagement over time because more engaged users are more likely to request access to the new design (or be granted access through CS tickets), leaving behind a holdout population skewed toward lower-engagement users; the distinguishing data would be composition analysis of holdout users over time (activity levels, tenure) compared to an enrolled holdout at each time point

The alternative explanation is that the metrics being measured (daily active use) are lagging indicators of long-term habit formation, and a 12-month gap of 4% represents the true sustained benefit while early higher gaps are noise; distinguishing data would be session-level behavioral depth metrics rather than top-line DAU
explanation: The most credible alternative explanation is holdout attrition bias through composition drift. Over 12 months, the most engaged and motivated users in the holdout group are most likely to notice they have a different experience, complain, seek the new design via customer support tickets, or use workarounds (e.g., switching devices). If these high-engagement users are preferentially leaving the holdout group — either by being moved to treatment or by churning from the platform entirely — the holdout population becomes increasingly composed of lower-engagement users over time. A holdout group shrinking in average engagement looks like the treatment-control gap is narrowing, when in reality the holdout baseline is deteriorating due to composition change. This is distinct from novelty decay (which would show treated user engagement declining back toward baseline rather than the control group declining toward treatment). The distinguishing data is composition analysis: if the holdout group's baseline engagement distribution is shifting toward lower values over 12 months while a freshly enrolled cohort shows stable distributions, composition drift is the likely explanation. Option A (social spillover) is possible but weak — the mechanism for significant behavioral adaptation without access to the new design is unclear. Option B (old design degradation) would show up in system metrics and is testable but less likely as a smooth, monotonic trend over 12 months. Option D mischaracterizes the pattern as noise and doesn't provide a mechanism for the decline.
hints: When a holdout group is maintained for 12 months, consider whether the composition of that holdout group might be changing over time — which users are most likely to leave the holdout, and what does that do to the group average?
Novelty decay means treatment users' behavior is returning toward a baseline — holdout composition drift means the control baseline itself is changing. What data would reveal each mechanism?

title: Holdout Group Cannibalization: Multi-Feature Attribution
scenario_context: A fintech app has maintained a 2% global holdout group for 18 months while the product team shipped 23 separate features. The holdout group now has 14% lower monthly active use than the treatment population. The team wants to attribute this 14% gap to individual features to prioritize which ones to invest in further. A data scientist proposes using the holdout group's single 14% gap to decompose feature contributions by correlating the timing of each feature launch with step changes in the holdout-vs-treatment gap over the 18 months. An experimentation researcher argues this approach has a fundamental flaw.
description: What is it?
options: The 2% holdout size is too small for reliable attribution analysis; individual feature contributions would have confidence intervals too wide to be actionable

The holdout group has been accumulating treatment-control divergence for 18 months — the features interact with each other over time, and users in the treatment group have been adapting their habits to the combined set of features for 18 months; attributing step changes in the gap to individual features ignores these interaction effects and the compounding of behavioral changes

Correlating step changes in the gap with launch timing conflates causation and correlation: a feature may launch during a period when the gap would have widened anyway due to seasonal effects or other confounders

The holdout group should have been replenished with new users every 6 months to remain representative; after 18 months, the holdout population is too different from the treatment population for any attribution analysis to be valid
explanation: The fundamental flaw is that the 14% gap reflects the combined, compounding effect of 23 features over 18 months — not the sum of 23 independent additive contributions. Users in the treatment group have been building habits, discovering features, and adapting their workflows in a holistic experience of all 23 features simultaneously. Features interact: a new search feature may become more valuable after a filtering feature is added; a notification feature's effect may depend on whether users have the mobile widget feature. Over 18 months, these interactions compound in ways that cannot be recovered by looking at step changes in the aggregate gap at each launch date. The step-change approach assumes that each feature's contribution is the discrete jump in the gap at its launch date and does not persist or interact with subsequent features — this is an unrealistic model of user behavior. Additionally, users in both groups are changing over time independently (tenure effects, seasonality), making causal attribution of step changes to specific features unreliable. Option A is a precision concern, not the fundamental flaw. Option C is a valid secondary concern about confounding but is not the core structural problem. Option D introduces a 'holdout replenishment' norm that is not standard and does not address the core attribution problem.
hints: When 23 features have been shipped to a single treatment group over 18 months, and users have been adapting to all of them simultaneously, can the cumulative gap be decomposed by feature using a step-change approach? Think about what assumption that requires.
Features shipped sequentially to a single population do not have independent effects — consider how user behavior adapts to a combined product experience over a long time horizon.

title: Combined Variance Reduction: CUPED and Stratification Interaction
scenario_context: A data scientist at a marketplace is designing an experiment on seller fee negotiation outcomes. She plans to use both stratified randomization (by seller GMV quintile) and a CUPED adjustment (using each seller's pre-experiment GMV as the covariate). She notes that the CUPED covariate (pre-experiment GMV) is strongly correlated with the stratification variable (GMV quintile, r ≈ 0.88). Her manager proposes dropping the CUPED adjustment since stratification already handles the GMV variation, and adding a second covariate — seller account age — to CUPED instead. The data scientist disagrees.
description: What is the most rigorous argument for her position?
options: The data scientist is right: CUPED should never be dropped even if the stratification variable is highly correlated, because CUPED additionally removes within-stratum variance that stratification does not address; dropping CUPED and replacing it with account age as the sole covariate would capture less variance unless account age has a higher within-stratum correlation with the outcome than pre-experiment GMV

The manager is right: when the stratification variable and CUPED covariate are highly correlated (r = 0.88), CUPED adds negligible variance reduction beyond stratification, and using a second independent covariate (account age) would provide more incremental variance reduction

The data scientist is right: it is always better to include more covariates in CUPED regardless of their correlation with the stratification variable, since additional covariates can only reduce or maintain variance and never increase it

The manager is right: double-adjusting for the same variance source (GMV) via both stratification and CUPED leads to over-controlling, which increases the standard error relative to using stratification alone
explanation: The data scientist's argument is correct and precise. Stratified randomization reduces between-stratum variance by ensuring each stratum has equal treatment/control proportions. However, within each stratum, there is still substantial variation in pre-experiment GMV — the stratification by quintile creates homogeneous groups in terms of rank but not in terms of continuous GMV values. CUPED uses the continuous pre-experiment GMV as a covariate, which removes variance at a finer granularity than the quintile strata. The two methods therefore address related but not identical variance: stratification removes between-stratum variance, CUPED additionally removes within-stratum variance that is correlated with the covariate. Even with r = 0.88 between the continuous covariate and the quintile variable, there is meaningful within-stratum variance remaining for CUPED to explain. The manager's proposal to replace pre-experiment GMV with account age in CUPED would only be better if account age has a higher within-stratum correlation with the outcome than pre-experiment GMV — which is unlikely since GMV is typically the strongest predictor of its own future values. Option B is approximately correct about the marginal gain from CUPED being reduced by stratification, but wrong to conclude it should be dropped. Option C is too absolute — covariates with negligible correlation with the outcome add variance through estimation rather than removing it. Option D incorrectly diagnoses 'over-controlling' as a risk in this context.
hints: Stratification removes variance between groups defined by the stratum, but within each stratum, variation remains. What can the pre-experiment covariate adjustment address that stratification alone cannot?
When the stratification variable and CUPED covariate are correlated but not identical (r = 0.88, not 1.0), think about whether CUPED is entirely redundant or still captures additional variance.

title: Interference Modeling: Equilibrium vs Local Treatment Effects
scenario_context: A food delivery platform tests a new driver incentive structure. Individual drivers are randomized: 40% receive new bonuses (treatment), 60% receive standard compensation (control). After 6 weeks, treatment drivers complete 12% more deliveries per day than control drivers. The platform wants to use this estimate to project the steady-state impact of rolling out the new incentive to all drivers. A senior economist argues that the 12% estimate cannot be directly used for this projection. The platform has a fixed pool of orders — there is no evidence the new incentive generates additional consumer demand.
description: What is the economist's argument, and is she correct?
options: The economist is wrong: the 12% lift is a valid direct estimate of the productivity gain from the new incentive structure, and rolling out to all drivers will yield a 12% platform-wide delivery increase

The economist is right: in the experiment, treatment drivers' additional completions come partly by capturing orders that would have been completed by control drivers; at full rollout with no control group, the total order pool is fixed, so the same 12% individual lift cannot materialize at the platform level — the equilibrium effect will be smaller and depends on the supply-demand response

The economist is right but only because the incentive increases driver costs; if the cost increase reduces driver supply at full rollout, the net platform-wide completions would fall below the current level

The economist is wrong: because individual driver productivity is measured at the individual level, equilibrium effects only matter for consumer-facing metrics like delivery time, not for driver-level completion rates
explanation: The economist is correct, and her argument is about the distinction between a partial equilibrium (experiment) estimate and a general equilibrium (full rollout) effect. In the experiment, 40% of drivers receive the new incentive and 60% do not. The treated drivers are more motivated to complete deliveries — they may accept orders faster, decline fewer requests, and work longer hours. In a marketplace with a fixed order pool, these additional completions by treated drivers come partly at the expense of control drivers, who receive fewer order opportunities because treated drivers are absorbing them first. The control group's completion rate is therefore artificially suppressed by competition from treated drivers, and the 12% gap is partly a within-experiment redistribution rather than a true productivity gain. At full rollout — when all drivers receive the new incentive — there are no control drivers to displace. The incremental completions cannot come from the same redistribution mechanism. The true platform-level effect depends on whether the incentive actually reduces driver idle time and churn (genuine productivity) versus simply redirecting orders among drivers. Option A ignores the supply-demand equilibrium structure of the marketplace. Option C raises a valid but different concern about cost and supply; this could be relevant but is not the economist's stated argument about the fixed order pool. Option D incorrectly claims equilibrium effects are only relevant for consumer-facing metrics — they are relevant for any metric measured in a shared resource environment.
hints: When treatment and control units compete for the same finite resource, what happens to the control group's access to that resource during the experiment — and what does that imply about the size of the measured effect?

Think about what changes when the experiment ends and the treatment is applied to everyone: which part of the treatment-control gap was driven by redistribution rather than genuine productivity, and does that part persist at full rollout?

title: Long-Run Holdout Group Decay: When the Counterfactual Diverges from Current Users
scenario_context: A major consumer tech platform maintains a permanent 5% holdout group excluded from all product feature launches. After two years of continuous feature deployment, the holdout group's weekly active usage is 23% lower than the treatment group. Product leadership declares a 23% cumulative lift from all features deployed over the two-year period. The data science team raises a validity concern about this attribution.
description: What is the primary validity concern with attributing the 23% usage gap to the cumulative effect of deployed features?
options: A two-year holdout group has experienced a fundamentally different product: no UX improvements, no recommendation updates, no performance work — users who found the unimproved product inadequate may have churned or severely reduced usage, leaving a survivor population that is self-selected and no longer representative of what current treatment users would look like without treatment; the 23% gap conflates the causal effect of features with compositional divergence and differential attrition between the two groups over time

The 23% estimate is directionally correct but should be time-discounted: features deployed in month 1 had 24 months to compound their effect while features deployed in month 23 had only 1 month; applying a time-weighted discount to each feature's individual contribution would reduce the headline 23% to a smaller but internally consistent cumulative lift estimate

The measurement is valid because the holdout group was randomly assigned two years ago; random assignment at baseline is sufficient for valid causal inference at any subsequent measurement horizon, regardless of how divergent the two groups' product experiences have become over the two-year period

The 23% gap underestimates the true feature impact: holdout users who churn do so because the inferior product fails to retain them, removing the least-engaged users and biasing the surviving holdout toward users who derive less incremental value from features; the true average treatment effect on the full user population is therefore larger than 23%
explanation:
Option A is correct. A holdout group's validity as a counterfactual rests on the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): holdout users' behavior must represent what treatment users would have done without treatment. Over two years, the holdout group experienced a product that fell progressively further behind the treatment product in quality. Users who needed improvements to stay engaged may have churned or reduced usage to accommodate the degraded experience. At the two-year mark, the holdout population is self-selected: survivors are those who tolerated an increasingly outdated product, a fundamentally different population from the average treatment user. Comparing treatment users (who received all features and retained engagement accordingly) against surviving holdout users confounds the causal feature effect with this compositional divergence and differential attrition.

Option B introduces time-value discounting, which is not a correction for compositional validity. The usage gap is a point-in-time measurement — current weekly active usage. Discounting individual feature contributions does not address the self-selection bias in the holdout population's composition at the measurement date.

Option C is wrong. Random assignment at baseline is necessary but not sufficient for valid long-run causal inference when the two groups have experienced radically different conditions and differential attrition for an extended period. Random assignment eliminates baseline confounding; it does not insulate against the compositional drift that occurs when the two groups experience different products and therefore exhibit different retention behavior over two years.

Option D's argument is plausible in structure but wrong in conclusion here. Whether heavy users benefit more or less from incremental features depends on feature type. More critically, Option D does not address the compositional validity concern — it accepts the gap as a valid causal estimate and merely debates its magnitude. The data science team's concern is about the validity of the comparison, not its direction.
hints: After two years without any product improvements, how likely is the holdout group's current composition and engagement level to represent what treatment users would look like without treatment? What has happened to holdout users who found the unimproved product inadequate?

Random assignment at the start of a holdout period ensures the groups are initially comparable. Does it guarantee they remain comparable after two years of experiencing different product quality, different recommendation quality, and different retention pressures?

title: Switchback Experiment Analysis: Temporal Autocorrelation Inflates the Test Statistic
code_snippet:
# Ride-share platform: 7-day switchback experiment
# Treatment/control alternates by day; ~200K active users/day
# Metric: average ride completions per user

periods = pd.DataFrame({
    'day':             [1,    2,    3,    4,    5,    6,    7],
    'treatment':       [1,    0,    1,    0,    1,    0,    1],
    'avg_completions': [4.82, 4.71, 4.85, 4.69, 4.79, 4.73, 4.83]
})

treat = periods[periods.treatment == 1]['avg_completions']
ctrl  = periods[periods.treatment == 0]['avg_completions']

from scipy.stats import ttest_ind
t_stat, p_val = ttest_ind(treat, ctrl)
print(f't={t_stat:.2f}, p={p_val:.3f}')  # Output: t=5.17, p=0.035
description: The t-test declares the experiment significant at α = 0.05 using 4 treatment periods and 3 control periods. A colleague argues this analysis is fundamentally flawed. What is the primary error, and what is the correct analytical approach?
options: The t-test treats 4 treatment days and 3 control days as 7 independent observations, but daily rideshare completions are serially autocorrelated — the same commuting patterns, weather, and events make adjacent days correlated regardless of treatment assignment; this autocorrelation means the effective sample size is much smaller than 7 and the standard error is underestimated, inflating the t-statistic and producing a false-positive; the correct approach uses cluster-robust or Newey-West standard errors that account for within-week temporal dependence, or a mixed-effects model with a random effect for time block

The fatal flaw is unequal group sizes: 4 treatment periods vs 3 control periods violates the equal-n requirement for a two-sample t-test; reassigning day 7 to control to achieve a balanced 3-vs-3 design eliminates the bias from the extra treatment observation

avg_completions is a ratio metric; all ratio statistics require delta method variance correction before a t-test is valid; ttest_ind significantly underestimates the variance for ratio metrics, inflating the t-statistic by approximately √n for a dataset of this size

A switchback experiment with only 7 periods cannot satisfy the Central Limit Theorem requirement for normality of period-level means; a minimum of 30 periods is required before the t-test approximation is valid; the result should be discarded and the experiment extended to at least 30 alternating periods
explanation:
Option A is correct. The standard independent-samples t-test assumes each observation is drawn independently from its population. In a time-series switchback experiment, daily averages are not independent — the same commuters travel on Monday and Tuesday, weekly seasonality (weekday vs weekend patterns) persists across adjacent days, and external shocks (weather, events) simultaneously affect consecutive days. Positive autocorrelation means observations share information: the effective number of independent data points is much smaller than 7. The t-test's standard error formula assumes independence and therefore underestimates the true standard error, inflating the t-statistic. The numerical pattern here (treatment days: 4.82, 4.85, 4.79, 4.83; control days: 4.71, 4.69, 4.73) is highly consistent within each group — a signature of correlated measurements, not independent sampling. The correct approach: cluster the standard errors at the day level (cluster-robust SE), apply Newey-West HAC correction, or use a mixed-effects model with a random intercept for time that absorbs the serial correlation before computing the treatment coefficient.

Option B is wrong. Unequal group sizes in a two-sample t-test do not bias the estimate — ttest_ind handles unequal n correctly by default using Welch's t-test. Reassigning an observation to achieve balance would reduce information. Unequal n is not a validity issue.

Option C applies to a different scenario. avg_completions here is the mean of a count metric computed over 200K users per day — not a ratio with a highly variable denominator. With 200K users per day, the CLT applies strongly to the daily mean, and the variance of the mean is well-estimated without delta method correction. The dominant error is autocorrelation, not ratio variance.

Option D is incorrect. There is no universal 30-period minimum for switchback experiments. The CLT approximation applies when observations are independent and the distribution of the test statistic converges — with positive autocorrelation, the problem is the violated independence assumption, not the period count. Even 100 periods of positively autocorrelated data would produce inflated t-statistics under a standard t-test.
hints: The t-test treats each day as an independent observation. In a rideshare market, is Tuesday's average ride count independent of Monday's? What shared factors create correlation between adjacent days in a time-series?

Positive autocorrelation between observations means consecutive measurements carry overlapping information — the effective sample size is smaller than the nominal count. How does overestimating the effective sample size affect the computed standard error and the resulting p-value?

title: Continuous monitoring with alpha spending: when can you stop early?
scenario_context: Your team implements a group sequential design with O'Brien-Fleming alpha spending across 4 equally-spaced looks (day 7, 14, 21, 28). The alpha boundaries are: look 1 z > 4.05 (p < 0.00005), look 2 z > 2.86 (p < 0.0021), look 3 z > 2.34 (p < 0.0097), look 4 z > 2.02 (p < 0.022). At day 14 (look 2), the observed z-score is 2.9. The PM wants to ship immediately.
description: Is stopping at look 2 valid, and what is the correct interpretation?
options: Stopping is not valid — you must wait until look 4; alpha spending only guarantees Type I error control at the final planned analysis, and early stopping always inflates the false-positive rate.
Stopping is valid: z = 2.9 exceeds the look-2 boundary of 2.86. The pre-specified alpha spending function preserves the overall Type I error rate regardless of which look triggers the stop.
Stopping is valid, but you must report the effect size as zero because the winner's curse means early-stopping estimates are always unreliable and cannot be reported.
Stopping is not valid — the conservative O'Brien-Fleming boundary at look 2 was designed to be almost never crossed in practice; a z = 2.9 crossing is most likely sampling noise.
explanation: Group sequential designs with alpha spending are explicitly built for valid early stopping at pre-specified interim analyses. The O'Brien-Fleming function allocates very little alpha to early looks (requiring very strong evidence at look 1) and progressively more to later looks, preserving the overall familywise Type I error at α. At look 2, z = 2.9 exceeds the pre-specified boundary of 2.86, so stopping is valid — the alpha budget is correctly allocated and the Type I error rate is controlled. Option A is false: the guarantee of Type I error control holds at each look, not just the final one — that is the definition of a valid alpha spending function. Option C is wrong: the winner's curse (upward bias in effect estimates at early stopping) is a real phenomenon that practitioners should account for, but the correction is to use an appropriate median-unbiased estimator or shrinkage estimate — not to report zero. Option D inverts the logic: the high boundary at look 2 is the mechanism that makes crossing it meaningful, not a sign that it was never intended to be crossed.
hints: Alpha spending pre-allocates portions of the total Type I error budget to each interim look. If z exceeds the look-2 boundary and that boundary was pre-specified, is the overall false-positive rate still controlled?
What distinguishes stopping early under a pre-specified alpha spending plan from the 'peeking' problem the plan was designed to prevent?
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Metric insensitivity: why your OEC hides a real treatment effect
scenario_context: A search team tests a re-ranking algorithm. Primary metric: revenue per query (RPQ). After 21 days with 500K queries per arm, RPQ shows +0.8% lift, p = 0.31, 95% CI [−0.7%, +2.3%]. Pre-experiment power analysis predicted 80% power for a 1% MDE. Post-analysis reveals: (1) 92% of queries produce zero revenue (informational queries), (2) the revenue-generating 8% has coefficient of variation 4.2 and kurtosis 38, (3) a parallel analysis on click-through rate (CTR, σ lower by 12×) shows +2.1% lift, p = 0.004. The team concludes the algorithm does not work.
description: Diagnose the flaw and identify what should change in future experiment design.
options: The conclusion is correct — CTR is a proxy metric; RPQ is the business metric and the null result is authoritative. Run the experiment longer.
The flaw is insufficient sample size — 500K queries per arm is too small; double the sample and rerun with the same metric.

The flaw is metric insensitivity: RPQ averages the zero-revenue query mass with a fat-tailed revenue distribution, structurally diluting any conversion effect. Future experiments should use a conditional metric (revenue per converting query) or a higher-sensitivity proxy (CTR, add-to-cart rate) as primary, with RPQ as a guardrail.
The flaw is novelty effect bias inflating the CTR result; the RPQ null result is the correct long-run estimate.
explanation: RPQ's composition — 92% zeros plus an extreme fat tail — makes it the wrong primary metric for detecting effects on the conversion funnel. The pre-experiment power calc assumed a σ inconsistent with this distributional structure. Averaging over the zero-revenue query mass dilutes the signal: any conversion gain affects only 8% of queries, and within that 8%, extreme variance means you need a sample roughly 100× larger than the 500K used. Doubling sample size (Option B) doesn't address the structural problem — at the observed σ, you remain severely underpowered. RPQ is not more 'authoritative' than CTR (Option A) — the question is whether it's the right instrument to measure the treatment's intended effect; here it demonstrably isn't. The novelty-effect explanation (Option D) is ad hoc: a novelty effect decays over weeks, but a 21-day experiment with sustained CTR lift is inconsistent with a novelty pattern. The correct design fix is to primary on conversion rate or CTR (which directly measures the algorithm's effect surface), use RPQ as a guardrail metric, and confirm revenue impact via a longer-running holdout if needed.
hints: If 92% of queries produce zero revenue, what fraction of the metric's signal is actually driven by the treatment? How does that fraction affect the effective signal-to-noise ratio?
What is the difference between 'the experiment was underpowered' and 'the metric definition structurally can't detect this class of effect at any feasible sample size'?

title: Churn prediction model targets wrong customers — what is the right causal framing?
scenario_context: A retention team trains a churn prediction model (AUC = 0.88) and plans to send a 30% discount to the top 10% of users by predicted churn probability. A data scientist argues this is the wrong approach. The predicted-churn segment includes: (A) users who will churn regardless of the discount, (B) users who won't churn regardless, (C) users who churn without the discount but stay with it, and (D) users who stay without the discount but would churn after receiving it (perceived as desperate).
description: What is the fundamental modeling flaw, and what is the correct approach?
options: The model's AUC is too low — retrain to achieve AUC > 0.95 before using it for targeting; a more accurate prediction model will correctly identify the right customers.

The flaw is that targeting high-predicted-churn customers conflates prediction with causation. The discount's causal effect (the lift in P(retain | discount) − P(retain | no discount)) is not captured by a churn prediction model. The model identifies who will churn (groups A and C mixed together), not who will respond to treatment (group C only — the Persuadables). The correct approach is uplift modeling: estimate the incremental causal effect of the discount on each customer using experimental data, and target only those with positive incremental uplift.
The approach is correct — high-churn-probability users are exactly the right targets for retention offers; the model is identifying the customers most at risk.
The flaw is targeting only 10%; expanding to 25% captures more true churners and improves ROI by reducing the per-saved-customer cost.
explanation: This is the fundamental distinction between predictive and causal modeling in a business context. A churn prediction model identifies *who will churn*, not *who will respond to a retention offer*. The four customer segments illustrate the problem: Segment A (Sure things — churn regardless) get the discount but can't be retained; this is wasted spend. Segment B (Lost causes — stay regardless) don't need the discount; this is margin erosion. Segment C (Persuadables — churn without discount, stay with it) are the only valuable targets — the treatment has positive incremental lift. Segment D (Do Not Disturbs — stay without discount, churn if offered) are actively harmed by targeting; the discount signals desperation and triggers cancellation. A churn prediction score mixes A and C (both are high-risk), completely missing the causal structure. Uplift modeling estimates P(retain | treatment) − P(retain | control) for each customer using past A/B experiment data, directly identifying Persuadables. Option A confuses prediction accuracy with causal validity — a perfect AUC churn model still targets wrong segments. Option C is the targeting fallacy being diagnosed. Option D addresses coverage without addressing the causal identification problem.
hints: A customer with 80% predicted churn probability who churns regardless of your offer: does giving them a discount improve your retention rate?
What experimental data structure would let you estimate the causal effect of a discount on each customer's retention probability?

title: PM wants to monitor a sequential test daily and stop whenever the line crosses — what goes wrong?
scenario_context: Your team implements an mSPRT sequential test with a target Type I error of 5%. The PM's understanding is: 'We can now check the dashboard every day and stop whenever the likelihood ratio exceeds the threshold.' On day 6 out of a planned 21-day window, the mSPRT statistic exceeds the threshold. The PM stops the experiment and ships. However, the experiment's power at day 6 is only 38% for the target 2% MDE.
description: Has the team used the sequential test correctly, and what is the power implication of stopping at day 6?
options: Yes, the team used the test correctly — mSPRT allows stopping at any point the threshold is crossed, and the Type I error guarantee holds regardless of when the stop occurs.

Stopping at day 6 is statistically valid under mSPRT (the Type I error guarantee does hold at any stopping time), but the practical implication is that the effect estimate is highly uncertain: at 38% power for a 2% MDE, a significant mSPRT crossing at day 6 is consistent with a real effect but also consistent with a large upward-biased estimate. The team should understand that early mSPRT stops produce winner's-curse-inflated effect estimates and plan accordingly.
The team used the test incorrectly — mSPRT requires pre-committing to a maximum sample and the test is only valid at that maximum, not at interim stops.
The test is invalid because 38% power is below the 80% threshold required for a valid sequential test to produce trustworthy results.
explanation: mSPRT (mixture Sequential Probability Ratio Test) is an anytime-valid inference method: the Type I error guarantee holds at every stopping time, not just at a pre-specified maximum. This is the core property that distinguishes mSPRT from a fixed-horizon test with interim looks. The stop at day 6 is therefore statistically valid — the false-positive rate is controlled at 5%. The practical concern is the power and effect-estimate reliability: at 38% power for a 2% MDE, a significant crossing on day 6 has a meaningful winner's curse component — the observed effect size is likely upward-biased from the true effect. The team should (1) treat the effect size estimate with appropriate caution, (2) communicate the uncertainty range, and (3) monitor post-ship metrics as a de facto holdout check. Option A is correct that stopping is valid but omits the crucial winner's curse caveat. Option C is wrong: mSPRT is specifically designed to avoid the 'must wait for maximum sample' requirement of fixed-horizon tests. Option D introduces a non-existent rule: there is no minimum power threshold for mSPRT validity; power is a design-time consideration (how long you'd expect to wait for a true effect), not a stopping-time validity condition.
hints: mSPRT's anytime-valid property means Type I error is controlled at every possible stopping time. What does that say about the validity of stopping at day 6?
At 38% power, if you stop at the first significant threshold crossing, what can you say about the expected bias of the effect estimate?

title: Group sequential with O'Brien-Fleming: predict whether stopping at look 3 is valid
scenario_context: An experiment uses O'Brien-Fleming alpha spending with 4 planned looks (days 7, 14, 21, 28) at overall α = 0.05. The pre-specified z-score thresholds are: look 1: z > 4.05, look 2: z > 2.86, look 3: z > 2.34, look 4: z > 2.02. At look 3 (day 21), z = 2.29. The PM notes: 'The z is very close to the threshold of 2.34 — can we call it significant given the closeness?'
description: Predict whether the look 3 result is statistically valid for stopping, and evaluate the PM's reasoning.
options: Yes — z = 2.29 is close to the threshold of 2.34, and in practice the difference is within rounding error of the data. Statistical thresholds are guidelines, not hard rules.

No — z = 2.29 does not exceed the pre-specified look-3 threshold of 2.34. The alpha spending function allocated exactly enough alpha to each look to keep the overall FWER at 5%; crossing 2.29 but not 2.34 means the alpha at look 3 has not been spent. The experiment must continue to look 4 with the lower final threshold of 2.02.
Stopping is valid because the experiment has already spent alpha at looks 1 and 2 without crossing; the unused alpha from those looks rolls over to look 3, reducing the threshold.
The result is borderline — apply a Bayesian posterior check at look 3; if posterior probability of improvement exceeds 95%, stop despite the frequentist miss.
explanation: The O'Brien-Fleming boundary at look 3 is exactly z > 2.34. z = 2.29 does not exceed this threshold, so the experiment has not reached the pre-specified stopping criterion at look 3. The alpha spending function pre-allocates the total Type I error budget across looks in a way that guarantees the overall FWER stays at 5% — it is not a 'guideline' to be rounded. Stopping at z = 2.29 would exceed the look-3 budget and inflate the overall Type I error. The correct path: continue to look 4, where the threshold is the more lenient z > 2.02. There, z = 2.29 would clearly exceed the threshold — so the team will very likely be able to stop at look 4 with the same data. The PM's 'rounding error' framing is the peeking fallacy in disguise: the threshold is exact, not approximate. Option C misunderstands alpha spending: unused alpha from not crossing earlier boundaries does NOT roll over to later looks. Each look's boundary is pre-specified and fixed. Option D applies Bayesian criteria to override a frequentist sequential design — mixing frameworks arbitrarily negates the FWER control guarantee of the sequential plan.
hints: Does z = 2.29 exceed the look-3 threshold of z > 2.34? What happens to the overall FWER if you stop at z = 2.29?
In an O'Brien-Fleming design, does failing to stop at an early look allow you to use a lower threshold at the next look?

title: Flat alpha spending vs O'Brien-Fleming: debug the power implication
scenario_context: A team designs a group sequential experiment with 4 looks and total α = 0.05. Instead of O'Brien-Fleming, they use a flat alpha spending function (equal α/4 = 0.0125 per look, threshold z > 2.24 at each look). A statistician argues this approach costs substantial power relative to O'Brien-Fleming. The team disagrees: 'We're using the same total α = 0.05 across all looks, so power should be the same.'
description: Who is correct, and why does the alpha spending shape affect power?
options: The team is correct — total alpha is fixed at 0.05 regardless of spending shape; power at the final analysis depends only on the total alpha budget, not its allocation.

The statistician is correct. Flat spending allocates α/4 = 0.0125 per look, requiring z > 2.24 to stop at any look. O'Brien-Fleming allocates much less alpha early (look 1: α ≈ 0.00005, z > 4.05) and more at the final look (α ≈ 0.022, z > 2.02). The final look threshold under flat spending (z > 2.24) is more conservative than O'Brien-Fleming's (z > 2.02), meaning flat spending has lower power at the final analysis. Total alpha is the same, but its shape changes the final-look threshold and therefore power.
Neither is fully correct — power depends on the true effect size, not the alpha spending shape; both designs have the same power if the true effect size is the same.
The statistician is wrong — flat spending is actually more powerful because it gives each look the same opportunity to stop, rather than concentrating alpha at the end.
explanation: Total alpha being equal (0.05) does not mean power is equal. Power depends on the specific threshold at the final analysis, not the total alpha budget. O'Brien-Fleming concentrates its alpha at the final look: the look-4 threshold under OBF is approximately z > 2.02 (p ≈ 0.022). Flat spending allocates α/4 = 0.0125 to each look, so the final-look threshold is z > 2.24 (p = 0.0125) — more conservative than OBF's 2.02. Since most experiments stop at the final look (early stopping requires very strong evidence), the power of the design is dominated by the final-look threshold. A stricter final threshold (2.24 vs 2.02) means lower power. OBF's design insight: protect early looks with very high thresholds (sacrificing almost no power) and preserve maximum power at the final look by concentrating alpha there. The team's intuition that 'same total alpha = same power' is wrong because alpha allocation shape directly determines the final-look critical value. Option A makes the incorrect 'total alpha = same power' argument. Option C correctly notes power depends on effect size but misses that for a fixed effect size, the alpha spending shape changes the rejection probability at each look. Option D inverts the logic: flat spending's equal early allocation uses alpha inefficiently, reducing power at the final analysis.
hints: What is the final-look z-threshold under flat spending (α/4 = 0.0125)? Under O'Brien-Fleming (α₄ ≈ 0.022)? Which threshold is easier to exceed?
If most experiments fail to stop early, which analysis (the final look) determines most of the power? How does the final-look threshold affect that?

title: Design a sequential experiment when business pressure peaks in week 2
scenario_context: Your team wants to detect a 3% lift on checkout conversion (σ = 22%). Standard fixed-horizon analysis requires 14 days (80% power, α = 0.05). The business has a Q4 deadline that creates maximum pressure to ship in week 2 (days 8–10). You propose a group sequential design with O'Brien-Fleming alpha spending and 2 looks: look 1 at day 8, final look at day 14.
description: Design the look-1 and look-2 thresholds and explain what the design buys relative to fixed-horizon.
options: Set both looks to z > 1.96 (the standard threshold) — sequential designs don't require changing the threshold if you pre-specify the looks.

With 2 looks at an O'Brien-Fleming-style spending, look 1 (day 8, 57% of information) should use a conservative threshold (z ≈ 2.80, p ≈ 0.005) and the final look (day 14) a slightly more conservative threshold than fixed-horizon (z ≈ 2.04, p ≈ 0.021). This design offers a valid early stop at day 8 if the effect is very strong, while preserving most of the fixed-horizon power at day 14 (≈76% vs 80%). The business gets a legitimate day-8 check-out with controlled Type I error.
Use a Pocock design (equal thresholds z ≈ 2.18 at both looks) — this maximises the chance of stopping at look 1 and gives the business the earliest possible decision.
Run the fixed-horizon test for 14 days without looks — interim looks always inflate Type I error and the business deadline should not drive statistical design.
explanation: An OBF 2-look design at the proposed interim/final split provides the best balance between business pressure and statistical validity. At 57% of information at look 1 (day 8 out of 14), OBF alpha spending allocates approximately α₁ ≈ 0.005 and α₂ ≈ 0.045, giving approximate z-thresholds of 2.80 and 2.04 respectively. The design has two key properties: (1) Type I error is controlled at 5% across both looks; (2) the final-look power (≈76%) is only slightly lower than fixed-horizon (80%), because the OBF design concentrates most of the alpha at the final look. The business gets a valid early-out on day 8 if the effect is very large (z > 2.80) without invalidating the final analysis. Option A is the peeking problem: using z > 1.96 at both looks without alpha spending would make the overall Type I error approximately 1 − (1 − 0.05)^2 ≈ 9.75%, not 5%. Option C (Pocock design) uses equal thresholds (z ≈ 2.18) — this makes look 1 more accessible, which sounds good for business pressure, but Pocock's final-look threshold (also 2.18) is more conservative than OBF's 2.04, reducing final-look power more. OBF is preferred when early stopping is expected to be infrequent and power preservation matters. Option D ignores the legitimate use case for a pre-specified sequential design when business constraints are real.
hints: How does OBF alpha spending allocate alpha between an early interim (57% of information) and a final analysis? Does the early interim get more or less alpha?
Pocock vs OBF: which preserves more power at the final analysis for a given overall α? Why?

title: Revenue per session as primary metric for a 1% conversion change — diagnose structural insensitivity
scenario_context: A team chooses revenue per session (RPS) as the primary metric for a checkout redesign experiment. Product data: 78% of sessions generate zero revenue; revenue-generating sessions have a heavy right tail (kurtosis = 24, σ = $38, mean = $4.20). The team targets a 1% relative conversion lift and runs a power analysis using the metric's full σ = $38 and mean = $4.20. Required sample: 3.6M sessions per arm. Daily traffic: 150K sessions. Estimated duration: 24 days.
description: Diagnose why RPS is structurally insensitive to a conversion rate change, and identify the better metric.
options: RPS is a valid primary metric; the high variance just requires more sample. The 24-day estimate is operationally acceptable.

RPS has two compounding insensitivity problems: (1) 78% zeros dilute the effect — a 1% conversion lift affects only the 22% non-zero sessions, so the lift on RPS from a 1% conversion lift is approximately 1% × 0.22 = 0.22% in expectation; (2) the heavy tail (kurtosis = 24) means the variance is driven by extreme sessions that are insensitive to the treatment, so you're comparing signal (0.22% lift) against noise dominated by unrelated outliers. Conversion rate avoids both problems: it has no zero-mass dilution and σ scales with √(p(1-p)) ≈ 0.18 at p = 12%, making it orders of magnitude more sensitive per observation.
The solution is to cap revenue at the 95th percentile to remove the heavy tail — winsorizing RPS will reduce variance enough to achieve the required sample size in under 14 days.
RPS is fine if you use a ratio metric estimator (delta method) to correct the standard error for the ratio structure — this accounts for the zeros and the heavy tail.
explanation: RPS is structurally insensitive to conversion rate changes for two compounding reasons. First, zero-mass dilution: 78% of sessions contribute zero to the metric regardless of treatment. A 1% lift on conversion rate moves only 22% of sessions; the implied effect on RPS is ~0.22%, not 1%. The signal is diluted by a factor of 4.5× before any variance is considered. Second, the heavy tail (kurtosis = 24) means the metric's variance is dominated by the top 1–5% of sessions — outlier spenders whose behavior is essentially independent of the checkout redesign. You're comparing a 0.22% signal against noise from unrelated high-value sessions. Conversion rate directly measures the treatment's first-order effect (does the redesign move users to purchase?) with variance bounded by p(1-p) ≈ 0.18², which is far more favorable. Option C (winsorizing) helps but doesn't fix the zero-mass dilution — capping at the 95th percentile removes outliers but the 78% zeros remain. You'd still need 3–5× more sample than conversion rate. Option D (delta method) corrects the standard error calculation for ratio structure but doesn't change the fundamental variance-driven insensitivity — a more precise standard error on a high-variance metric still requires more data.
hints: A 1% conversion lift on sessions that are 78% zero-revenue: what is the implied lift on revenue per session in expectation? How does that affect your signal-to-noise ratio?
Kurtosis = 24 means extreme values dominate the variance. Are those extreme-value sessions sensitive to a checkout redesign?

title: Log-revenue vs raw revenue in a skewed distribution — when does log-transformation help and when does it mask?
scenario_context: Your team tests a subscription pricing change. Revenue per user has extreme right skew (kurtosis = 18, 95th percentile = $220, median = $12, mean = $31). You apply log(1 + revenue) as the metric. Log-revenue variance drops from σ² = 1840 to σ² = 2.1. The required sample size drops from 2.8M to 3,200 per arm. The transformation makes the experiment 875× more efficient.
description: What does the log-transformation achieve, and what must the team be careful about in interpretation?
options: Log-transformation is always valid for right-skewed revenue data — the efficiency gain is real and the results are fully interpretable on the original revenue scale by exponentiating the estimate.

Log-transformation effectively removes the heavy tail's influence on variance, making the experiment highly sensitive to multiplicative changes in revenue. The 875× efficiency gain is genuine. However, the treatment effect is now estimated on the log scale — the reported estimate is a relative (multiplicative) lift in geometric mean revenue, not an absolute dollar lift in mean revenue. The team must be clear: they are measuring whether revenue is higher by a constant factor, not whether mean revenue increased by a specific dollar amount. Absolute dollar lift on mean revenue requires a separate analysis.
The transformation is invalid because log(1 + revenue) is not a pre-registered metric; using it after observing the variance reduction is HARKing.
The efficiency gain is misleading — the 875× reduction in required sample reflects a change in what is being measured, not a genuine power improvement for the business question.
explanation: Log-transformation is a legitimate variance-reduction technique for heavily right-skewed revenue metrics. By transforming to log(1 + revenue), the extreme outliers are compressed and the metric's variance drops dramatically (from 1840 to 2.1) — this is real and produces a genuine reduction in required sample. The critical interpretation constraint: the treatment effect on log-revenue is an estimate of the multiplicative effect on geometric mean revenue. If log(1 + revenue) increases by δ, then geometric mean revenue increases by a factor of e^δ − 1. This is not the same as the mean revenue change. For a pricing test, the business cares about total revenue impact (which depends on mean revenue, not geometric mean). Both are legitimate metrics, but they answer different questions. The team must communicate clearly which they are measuring. Option A is partly right about the efficiency but wrong about interpretability: exponentiating the log estimate gives the geometric mean ratio, not the mean revenue ratio — these are different in the presence of skew. Option C incorrectly frames a pre-transformation metric choice as HARKing — if log-revenue is a legitimate metric for the question (and it is for multiplicative pricing effects), pre-specifying it is correct practice, not HARKing. Option D is incorrect: the efficiency gain is real in the sense that the log-metric captures the pricing test's effect with much higher sensitivity; the concern about 'what is being measured' is valid but leads to careful interpretation, not dismissal.
hints: The mean of log(X) is not the log of the mean of X. When you estimate an effect on log-revenue, what does exponentiating the estimate give you — and how is that different from mean revenue?
Is the 875× efficiency gain 'real'? In what sense yes, and in what sense does it come with a measurement tradeoff?

title: Two metrics with different variance structures — predict sample size ratio
scenario_context: Your team needs to detect a 2% relative lift on two candidate metrics: Metric A: revenue per session (mean = $5.00, σ = $42, CV = 8.4). Metric B: conversion rate (mean = 0.12, σ = 0.325, CV = 2.7). MDE for both: 2% relative lift (δ_A = $0.10, δ_B = 0.0024). Power = 80%, α = 0.05.
description: Predict the ratio of required sample sizes (n_A / n_B) and what this implies for experiment design.
options: n_A / n_B ≈ 3.1 — revenue has 3× the CV of conversion rate (8.4 vs 2.7), so squaring gives roughly 9.7×, but the CV shortcut is only valid when δ is expressed as an absolute value, not a relative lift; the correct approach uses the direct (σ/δ)² formula giving 3.1×.

n_A / n_B ≈ 9.6 — required n ∝ (σ/δ)². For metric A: (σ_A / δ_A)² = ($42 / $0.10)² = 420² = 176,400. For metric B: (σ_B / δ_B)² = (0.325 / 0.0024)² = 135.4² = 18,333. Ratio: 176,400 / 18,333 ≈ 9.6. The CV-ratio shortcut is not applicable here because the two metrics use different units (dollars vs probability); the direct formula is the only valid approach.

n_A / n_B ≈ 9.7 — the CV ratio squared (8.4 / 2.7)² = 9.7 is the correct and complete answer. The direct (σ/δ)² calculation is unnecessary when CV data is available; computing it separately adds no precision.

n_A / n_B ≈ 9.6–9.7 — both the direct (σ/δ)² method and the CV-ratio shortcut are valid approaches that converge on approximately 10×. The practical implication is that revenue experiments require ~10× more data than conversion experiments at a 2% relative MDE — meaning weeks rather than days at typical traffic levels.
explanation:
Required sample size ∝ (σ/δ)² at fixed α and power. For a relative MDE of 2%, δ = 0.02 × mean. For metric A: δ_A = 0.02 × $5.00 = $0.10; (σ_A/δ_A)² = ($42/$0.10)² = 420² = 176,400. For metric B: δ_B = 0.02 × 0.12 = 0.0024; (σ_B/δ_B)² = (0.325/0.0024)² ≈ 135.4² ≈ 18,333. Ratio: 176,400 / 18,333 ≈ 9.6. The CV-ratio shortcut: (CV_A/CV_B)² = (8.4/2.7)² ≈ 9.7, which matches because when MDE is expressed as a relative lift, (σ/δ)² = (σ/(r·μ))² = (CV/r)², so the ratio n_A/n_B = (CV_A/CV_B)² — the relative MDE r cancels. Both methods are valid and agree.

Option D is the most complete and correct answer: it gives the right numerical range (≈9.6–9.7 ≈ 10×), confirms both calculation methods yield the same result, and states the practical implication (10× longer experiments for revenue).

Option A is wrong: the claim that the CV shortcut is invalid for relative MDEs is incorrect. The CV shortcut is precisely valid for relative MDEs — the CV (σ/mean) and the relative MDE (r = δ/mean) combine to give (σ/δ)² = (CV/r)², so the ratio n_A/n_B = (CV_A/CV_B)² when r is the same for both metrics. The stated ratio of 3.1× is wrong.

Option B gives the correct numerical answer (≈9.6) via the direct formula but incorrectly dismisses the CV shortcut as inapplicable. The CV shortcut is fully valid here, and cross-checking both methods is better practice than relying on only one.

Option C gives the correct ratio via the CV shortcut but incorrectly dismisses the direct (σ/δ)² formula as unnecessary. Both approaches should be used; cross-validation is a professional discipline check, not redundancy.
hints: Required sample size ∝ (σ/δ)². For a relative MDE of 2%, δ = 0.02 × mean. Compute (σ/δ) for each metric and square the ratio.
The CV (σ/mean) captures the relative noise. If the MDE is also expressed as a relative lift, how does CV directly determine sample size requirements?

title: Fuzzy RDD: the eligibility threshold is not perfectly enforced — what does this mean for your estimate?
scenario_context: Your team wants to use regression discontinuity design (RDD) to estimate the causal effect of a credit limit increase on customer spending. The policy: users above a credit score of 700 automatically get a $500 credit increase. However, your data shows: (a) 15% of users with score > 700 did not receive the increase (manual review exceptions), (b) 8% of users with score < 700 did receive it (manager overrides). Compliance at the threshold is approximately 77%.
description: How does imperfect compliance at the threshold affect the RDD estimate?
options: The non-compliance makes the RDD invalid — imperfect threshold enforcement means the discontinuity cannot be used for causal identification.

Imperfect compliance converts the design from a sharp RDD to a fuzzy RDD. The running variable (credit score) still determines assignment probability, but not deterministically. In a fuzzy RDD, the estimated causal effect is a local average treatment effect (LATE) for compliers — users near the threshold whose treatment status actually changes with the running variable. The estimate is scaled by 1/compliance: if the ITT (intent-to-treat) estimate is X, the LATE is approximately X / 0.77. The LATE is a valid causal estimate, but for a more restricted sub-population (compliers near the threshold, not all users).
Imperfect compliance is fine — average out the non-compliers across both sides of the threshold and proceed with a standard sharp RDD analysis.
Use an IV approach instead of RDD: instrument the credit increase with the credit score threshold. This fully resolves the non-compliance problem.
explanation: A fuzzy RDD exists when treatment probability is discontinuous at the threshold but not a step function from 0 to 1. The credit score threshold at 700 creates a jump in P(treatment): below 700, ~8% get the increase; above 700, ~85% get it — a compliance rate of ~77%. In a fuzzy RDD, the standard sharp RDD estimator (ratio of outcome discontinuity to treatment discontinuity at the threshold) gives the LATE for compliers: those whose treatment status is driven by the running variable, not by override decisions. This is a valid and well-defined causal estimate, but it applies to a more restricted population than sharp RDD. The estimate is also less precise because the first stage (treatment discontinuity) is weaker (77% vs 100% compliance). Option A is too categorical — fuzzy RDD is a recognized, valid design; 'imperfect compliance = invalid' is wrong. Option C (average out non-compliers) would give an ITT estimate without scaling by compliance — valid but has a different interpretation (it measures the effect of eligibility, not the effect of treatment). Option D is partially correct: IV with the threshold as instrument is mathematically equivalent to fuzzy RDD at the threshold — they give the same LATE estimate. But 'use IV instead' is not a resolution; it's the same estimator described differently.
hints: What is the difference between sharp RDD (perfect compliance) and fuzzy RDD (imperfect compliance) in terms of what the estimator identifies?
If 77% of eligible users actually receive treatment, how does the fuzzy RDD estimate relate to the intent-to-treat estimate?

title: Holdout group reveals 14-day A/B read missed 60% of the long-run effect
scenario_context: A team launches a personalization algorithm and maintains a 5% holdout group. The initial 14-day A/B test showed +1.8% retention lift. At 6 months, the holdout analysis shows +4.6% retention lift. The PM asks: 'Did our A/B test fail to detect the real effect?'
description: How should you interpret the 14-day vs 6-month divergence, and what does it imply about the 14-day read's validity?
options: The 14-day read was correct — the algorithm improved by +2.8 percentage points over 6 months due to personalization model retraining, which is a different effect than the original A/B.

The 14-day and 6-month estimates measure fundamentally different quantities: the 14-day A/B measures the short-run causal effect of the initial algorithm (real and valid); the 6-month holdout measures the long-run effect, which can be larger due to compounding model improvements, engagement flywheel effects, and network-benefit accumulation that take months to manifest. Neither read is 'wrong' — they answer different causal questions about different time horizons. The implication: the 14-day A/B was not a measurement failure; it correctly captured the early effect. The holdout provides the long-run causal estimate that the short A/B cannot.
The 14-day A/B was underpowered — if it had run for 6 months it would have detected +4.6% directly, with no holdout needed.
The holdout result is biased upward because holdout users are increasingly different from treated users over 6 months due to selection effects; the 14-day A/B is the more reliable estimate.
explanation: The divergence between short-run A/B and long-run holdout is expected and does not indicate a measurement failure. The 14-day A/B captured the immediate causal effect of switching from the old to the new algorithm — a real, valid estimate for its time horizon. The long-run holdout captures compounding mechanisms: (1) the personalization model trains on new user data, improving over time in treatment but not in holdout; (2) users in treatment develop engagement patterns that compound (returning more often, building preferences that improve recommendations further); (3) content producers may adjust to the algorithm, increasing the quality of recommended content. These are real long-run causal effects that a short-horizon A/B by design cannot capture. The holdout group answers: 'What is the 6-month causal effect of this system?' — which is different from the 14-day question. Option A correctly notes model retraining as one mechanism but frames it as a 'correction' to the A/B rather than a different quantity being measured. Option C mistakes the long-run effect for something a longer A/B would have detected — a 6-month A/B would measure long-run effects but at the cost of delaying launch and without the compounding benefits of the launched product. Option D raises selection bias in holdouts (holdout users' behavior diverges over time), which is a real concern, but the solution is accounting for this, not dismissing the holdout.
hints: A 14-day A/B measures the short-run effect of a fixed algorithm state. What mechanisms can cause the long-run effect to be larger?
Is a holdout group measuring the same causal quantity as a 14-day A/B? If not, which is 'right'?
