title: 40% of holdout users accessed treatment via referral links — assess the contamination bias
scenario_context: A team maintains a 10% holdout group to measure the long-run effect of a new social sharing feature. After 3 months, data shows: 40% of holdout users received referral links from treatment users and saw the feature-gated shared content (though they could not use the feature's active components). Holdout users who clicked referral links showed 12% higher retention than holdout non-clickers. The overall holdout comparison (vs treatment) shows +2.1% retention lift for treatment.
description: In which direction does the referral-link contamination bias the treatment effect estimate?
options: Upward bias — holdout users who see shared content are exposed to positive feature experiences, making holdout retention higher than it would be in a clean holdout. This makes the treatment-vs-holdout gap appear smaller, not larger.

Downward bias — the contaminated holdout users have higher retention (12% above non-clickers), which inflates the holdout comparison group's retention rate. A higher holdout baseline means the treatment lift estimate (treatment minus holdout) is smaller than the true causal effect — the +2.1% underestimates the true long-run effect.
No systematic bias — referral-link exposure affects both high-engagement and low-engagement holdout users equally, so the holdout group remains representative.
The bias direction is indeterminate — referral links could increase holdout engagement (upward bias) or create jealousy/frustration at being locked out (downward bias).
explanation: The contamination is downward-biasing the treatment effect estimate. The causal chain: holdout users who receive referral links (40%) have 12% higher retention — they are partially benefiting from the treatment's social spillover (seeing shared content, staying engaged with the ecosystem). This raises the holdout group's retention rate above what a clean holdout would show. The treatment effect is estimated as (treatment retention) − (holdout retention). If holdout retention is inflated by spillover, the gap shrinks — the +2.1% observed is a lower bound on the true causal effect. The contamination mechanism is called 'spillover' or 'interference': the treatment's benefits leak to holdout users through the social sharing network, violating SUTVA. Option A confuses the direction: spillover raises the holdout group's retention, which narrows the treatment-holdout gap, not widening it. Option C is wrong — referral links selectively reach higher-engagement users (those with treatment social connections), creating a non-representative enriched holdout sample. Option D cites frustration as an alternative mechanism — while theoretically possible, the data shows 12% higher retention in referral-link clickers, which is evidence of positive spillover, not frustration.
hints: If holdout users' retention is partially elevated by spillover from treatment, does that make the holdout control group's baseline higher or lower than a clean control?
Treatment effect = treatment retention − holdout retention. If holdout retention is inflated by spillover, what happens to the measured treatment effect?

title: Bayesian shows 95% probability of improvement but frequentist p = 0.07 — how do you reconcile this for the PM?
scenario_context: Your team runs parallel Bayesian and frequentist analyses on a checkout experiment. Frequentist: +1.6% conversion lift, 95% CI [−0.1%, +3.3%], p = 0.07. Bayesian (flat prior): posterior probability of positive effect = 96.5%, posterior median = +1.7%, 95% credible interval [+0.05%, +3.35%]. The PM asks: 'Bayesian says 96.5% likely to be positive, frequentist says not significant — which do I use for my ship decision?'
description: Reconcile the two results and provide a defensible ship/no-ship recommendation.
options: Use the Bayesian result — 96.5% probability of improvement is high enough for a business decision; the frequentist threshold is overly conservative.

The two results are more consistent than they appear. The frequentist CI [−0.1%, +3.3%] and the Bayesian credible interval [+0.05%, +3.35%] are nearly identical — the practical uncertainty is the same. The difference is the decision framework: frequentist p = 0.07 means 'if there is no effect, observing this result 7% of the time' (not the probability that the effect is positive); the Bayesian posterior directly estimates the probability the effect is positive at 96.5% given the flat prior. With a flat prior, this means 96.5% of the posterior mass is above zero — almost identical to 1 − (0.07/2) from the CI interpretation, approximately. The right question is: does the business value a 1.7% expected lift at an acceptable posterior risk? If the cost of a false positive is low relative to the expected gain, 96.5% posterior is sufficient. Define the decision criterion before interpreting either result.
Use the frequentist result — Bayesian analysis requires informative priors; a flat prior is not appropriate for a business context and invalidates the 96.5% claim.
The results are contradictory — run more sample until both methods agree before making a decision.
explanation: The apparent contradiction dissolves under careful interpretation. The frequentist CI [−0.1%, +3.3%] and Bayesian credible interval [+0.05%, +3.35%] are nearly numerically identical — they express the same uncertainty about the effect. The difference is what they mean: the Bayesian posterior P(effect > 0) = 96.5% is a direct probability statement about the parameter; the frequentist p = 0.07 is the probability of observing this data (or more extreme) under the null. With a flat prior, the Bayesian analysis with a one-sided frequentist test are nearly equivalent: p/2 ≈ 0.035, and 1 − 0.035 ≈ 96.5% — confirming consistency. The decision depends on the business context, not the statistical framework: at 96.5% posterior probability of a positive effect with expected value +1.7%, the ship decision depends on whether the cost of a false ship (3.5% chance of a null or negative effect) is tolerable relative to the expected gain. Option A cherry-picks the Bayesian result without explaining why the frequentist result doesn't contradict it. Option C is wrong: flat priors are a legitimate and commonly used choice in Bayesian analysis; they represent maximal prior ignorance and produce the most data-driven posteriors. Option D recommends more data without recognizing that the results are already consistent.
hints: With a flat prior, the Bayesian 95% credible interval and the frequentist 95% CI should be numerically similar. Are they, in this case?
If the frequentist CI barely includes zero (lower bound = −0.1%) and the Bayesian posterior P(positive) = 96.5%, are these consistent or contradictory? What explains the relationship?

title: Posterior 95% credible interval [+0.5%, +2.3%] — predict the correct interpretation vs frequentist CI
scenario_context: A Bayesian A/B test (uninformative prior) produces a posterior distribution over the conversion rate lift. The 95% posterior credible interval (CrI) is [+0.5%, +2.3%]. A frequentist analysis of the same data produces a 95% CI of [+0.5%, +2.3%] (identical bounds). The PM asks: 'What is the difference between the Bayesian and frequentist intervals if they have the same numbers?'
description: Predict the correct interpretation of each interval and the key difference in meaning.
options: No difference — if the intervals have the same bounds, they make the same claim. The Bayesian and frequentist intervals are interchangeable in practice.

The bounds are numerically the same (due to a flat prior making the posterior ≈ the likelihood), but the interpretations differ fundamentally. The frequentist 95% CI means: 'If we repeated this experiment many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter.' It does NOT mean there is a 95% probability that the true effect is in [+0.5%, +2.3%]. The Bayesian 95% CrI means: 'Given the data and prior, there is a 95% probability that the true effect is in [+0.5%, +2.3%].' The Bayesian interpretation is the one most people intuitively want from an interval.
The frequentist CI is valid only for large samples (n > 30); the Bayesian CrI is valid for any sample size. With identical bounds, the Bayesian interval is always preferred.
The frequentist CI refers to future experiments; the Bayesian CrI refers to the current experiment. They answer different time-horizon questions.
explanation: When a flat (uninformative) prior is used, the Bayesian posterior is proportional to the likelihood, making the credible interval numerically identical to the confidence interval. But the interpretations are different. The frequentist CI is a statement about the procedure's long-run behavior: 'If the experiment were repeated many times under the same setup, 95% of the computed intervals would contain the true effect.' It does not say the probability that the true effect is in this specific interval is 95% — the true effect is fixed, not random, in frequentist statistics. The Bayesian CrI is a direct probability statement about the parameter: 'Given the observed data and the prior, the probability that the true effect lies in [+0.5%, +2.3%] is 95%.' This is the natural interpretation people want. Both are valid, but they answer different questions. The practical difference matters most when (1) the prior is not flat (informative Bayesian priors pull the CrI toward prior beliefs), or (2) you want to directly say 'the probability is X' — only the Bayesian framework licenses that statement. Option A is wrong despite being practically tempting: identical bounds with different interpretations are not equivalent statements. Option C confuses sample-size requirements with framework validity. Option D mischaracterizes the frequentist CI as about future experiments — it's about the long-run behavior of the interval-generating procedure.
hints: In frequentist statistics, is the 'true effect' a fixed quantity or a random variable? How does that affect what a CI can claim about probability?
Which interpretation — frequentist CI or Bayesian CrI — licenses the statement 'there is a 95% probability the effect is in this range'?

title: DiD shows +5% effect but parallel trends is violated — what does this mean for the causal claim?
scenario_context: A policy team uses difference-in-differences (DiD) to estimate the effect of a new discount program on customer spending. Treatment: users in cities A, B, C (program rolled out). Control: users in cities D, E, F (no program). Pre-period trends: treatment group spending grew at 8% per month; control group spending grew at 3% per month. The DiD estimate at 3 months: +5% spending lift in treatment vs control.
description: What does the violation of parallel trends mean for the +5% estimate?
options: The +5% estimate is valid — DiD compares the change in the treatment group to the change in the control group, which corrects for any baseline difference between groups.

Parallel trends violation means the two groups were on divergent trajectories before the treatment. DiD assumes treatment and control would have had the same trend absent the treatment — if treatment cities were already growing at 8% vs control's 3%, the 5% DiD estimate confounds the program effect with the pre-existing 5% per month trend difference. The estimated causal effect cannot be isolated from this pre-existing divergence.
The parallel trends violation only matters if the pre-period trend difference (8% vs 3%) is statistically significant; if the difference in pre-trends is not significant, the DiD estimate is valid.
DiD is still valid — the parallel trends assumption requires that groups trend similarly, not identically; a 5% difference in monthly growth rate is within normal variation.
explanation: The parallel trends assumption requires that in the absence of treatment, treatment and control would have followed the same time trend. Pre-period evidence of divergent trends (8% vs 3% monthly growth, a 5 percentage-point divergence) means this assumption is violated. The DiD estimator is (ΔY_treatment − ΔY_control), which implicitly attributes all differential change to the treatment. If treatment cities were already growing faster, the 5% DiD estimate mixes the program's causal effect with the pre-existing trend difference. The estimated +5% could reflect the program working, or the continuation of the trend divergence, or both — it is unidentifiable from the DiD design alone. Possible remedies: (1) use a synthetic control that matches pre-trends, (2) use a longer pre-period to test trend stability, (3) apply a continuous DiD model with trend controls. Option A misunderstands what DiD corrects for — it corrects for level differences between groups (different baselines), not trend differences. Option C introduces a null-hypothesis test on pre-trends as the validity criterion — this is common in practice but is a statistical test with finite power; non-significance doesn't imply parallel trends hold. Option D redefines 'same trend' as 'similar enough,' which is not the assumption — the assumption is that the counterfactual trend is parallel, and evidence of pre-period divergence directly contradicts this.
hints: DiD removes time-invariant group differences. Does it also remove pre-existing trend differences between groups?
If treatment cities were already growing 5 percentage points faster per month before the program, what would the DiD estimate show even if the program had zero causal effect?

title: DiD control group differs in 3 demographic dimensions — identify the bias source
scenario_context: A team estimates the effect of a loyalty program using DiD. Treatment cities received the program; control cities did not. Post-hoc analysis reveals: control cities have (a) 18% higher median income, (b) 35% lower urban density, (c) 22% younger median age than treatment cities. The DiD estimate shows +7% spend lift. A reviewer says the estimate is biased.
description: Which demographic differences create bias in the DiD estimate, and what is the direction?
options: Demographic differences between groups do not bias DiD — DiD differences out all time-invariant group characteristics, including demographic composition.

Level differences (higher income, different density, younger age) are differenced out by DiD as time-invariant group fixed effects. The bias arises if these demographic differences produce different trends over time — for example, if high-income cities respond differently to macroeconomic conditions, or if younger populations have different spending trajectories. The demographic gap creates a risk of parallel trends violation, not a mechanical level bias. The direction of bias depends on whether the differenced trends favour treatment or control.

All three differences bias the DiD estimate upward — control cities have characteristics (higher income, lower density, younger age) that produce higher baseline spending, which makes the treatment look worse by comparison.
Only the income difference matters — density and age are not correlated with spending growth and do not affect the DiD estimate.
explanation: DiD removes group-level time-invariant differences — this is its key identification property. If treatment and control cities differ in income, density, and age at baseline, DiD differences these out through the before-after comparison. The bias risk is not from level differences but from differential trends caused by those demographic differences. For example: (a) High-income control cities may respond differently to the same macroeconomic shock (divergent trend); (b) Low-density control areas may have different retail seasonality (non-parallel seasonal trends); (c) Younger control populations may have different spending growth trajectories over the measurement period. Any of these can invalidate the parallel trends assumption — the demographic differences are the mechanism by which trends might diverge. The bias direction depends on the interaction between the demographic gaps and the time trends. Option A is partially correct (level differences are differenced out) but misses the trend-divergence risk. Option C describes a level bias that DiD specifically removes — it incorrectly applies static comparison logic to a difference-in-differences design. Option D oversimplifies — density and age can affect spending trends (not just levels), and all three gaps are potential trend-divergence risks.
hints: DiD removes time-invariant group differences (levels). What kind of group difference does DiD NOT remove?
If high-income control cities respond differently to macroeconomic shocks than lower-income treatment cities, what does that imply about the parallel trends assumption?

title: Marketplace with 40% buyer-seller overlap: why user-level randomization biases the estimate
scenario_context: A marketplace platform tests a new seller-tools feature. 40% of buyers are also sellers on the platform. User-level randomization: treatment sellers get the new tools; control sellers do not. After 14 days, the primary metric (buyer GMV) shows +2.8% lift (p = 0.018). A skeptic argues the estimate is biased due to buyer-seller interference.
description: Explain the SUTVA violation and predict the direction of bias.
options: No violation — treatment sellers are assigned to treatment and control buyers are separate users; there is no crossover.

SUTVA is violated because 40% of buyers are also sellers. A buyer who is in the control arm for buyers may be in the treatment arm for sellers — they use the new tools as a seller, which improves their listings and product quality. Their buyer behavior (spending as buyers) may be affected by their improved seller experience. Control buyers who are also sellers in treatment experience improved marketplace quality as sellers but are counted as 'control' buyers. This inflates the control group's GMV (control buyers who are treatment sellers buy more), narrowing the treatment-control gap and underestimating the true treatment effect.
SUTVA is violated and the bias is upward — treatment sellers improve their listings, attracting more buyers from the control arm into the marketplace, inflating treatment GMV.
The violation creates bidirectional bias that cannot be determined without further analysis of the buyer-seller overlap network.
explanation: The buyer-seller overlap creates a classic SUTVA violation: a user's potential outcome as a buyer is not independent of the treatment assignment of other users (specifically, the sellers they interact with). The mechanism: treatment sellers have improved tools → they create better listings → buyers (including control buyers who happen to be treatment sellers themselves) benefit from improved marketplace quality. The 40% who are both buyers and sellers are in treatment (seller arm) and potentially in control (buyer arm) simultaneously — their GMV as buyers is elevated by their seller-arm treatment status. This inflates the control arm's buyer GMV, narrowing the treatment-control gap. Implication: the +2.8% GMV lift understates the true causal effect of the seller tools. The correct design: geo-cluster or marketplace-cluster randomization, assigning entire local markets to treatment or control. Option A is wrong — the buyer-seller overlap creates a direct channel for treatment spillover into the control arm via user identity. Option C describes a different mechanism (attracting more buyers into the marketplace, a supply-side effect) — valid in principle but conflates the mechanism and direction; the primary bias is through the buyer-seller overlap contaminating the control arm, not through attracting new buyers. Option D defers when the direction is actually determinable from the mechanism.
hints: If a user is assigned to control as a buyer but to treatment as a seller, which arm does their buyer GMV get counted in? What does their improved seller experience do to their buyer behavior?
If control buyers' GMV is elevated by the 40% who are also treatment sellers, is the treatment-control gap larger or smaller than the true effect?

title: SRM with +3% lift: PM says 'fix the routing and the lift will hold' — evaluate this
scenario_context: A checkout redesign experiment shows +3.1% conversion lift (p = 0.009). SRM check: 53.8% control / 46.2% treatment (chi-squared p = 6 × 10^-15). Investigation reveals the cause: a CDN caching bug routes users reaching checkout via organic search to control at a higher rate. Organic-search users convert at 5.2% vs direct-navigation users at 2.8%. The PM proposes: 'Fix the CDN bug, re-randomize, and the +3.1% lift will hold — the algorithm clearly works.'
description: Evaluate the PM's reasoning and predict what the corrected estimate is likely to be.
options: The PM is correct — fixing the CDN bug removes the randomization problem, and the true effect will be close to +3.1% since the treatment is genuinely better.

The PM's reasoning is flawed. The SRM over-routes high-converting users (organic-search, 5.2% conversion) to control, inflating control's conversion rate. The +3.1% lift is largely an artifact of the biased comparison. After correcting the bug and re-randomizing, the true effect is likely much smaller — possibly near zero. The PM is mistaking correlation for causation.
The PM is partially right — fix the bug and re-randomize. The true lift will be between +1.5% and +3.1% because only part of the effect is due to the SRM bias.
The PM is wrong for a different reason: the CDN bug affects both arms equally, so the direction of lift is also wrong — the true effect could be negative.
explanation: The SRM is caused by systematically routing high-converting users (organic-search, 5.2% conversion) to control. This means control has a disproportionate share of high-intent users, inflating its conversion rate above what a fair 50/50 split would show. The treatment group underrepresents organic-search users and has a lower baseline conversion rate. The measured +3.1% lift is the difference between an inflated control and a deflated treatment — it may entirely reflect the user-composition difference rather than any causal effect of the redesign. After fixing the bug and re-randomizing with balanced assignment, organic-search users will be equally represented in both arms, raising control's denominator quality and likely eliminating or greatly reducing the apparent lift. The PM's 'the algorithm clearly works' conclusion is invalid — you cannot read causality from a biased experiment. Option A accepts the PM's reasoning by assuming bug removal preserves the estimate. Option C acknowledges bias but speculates a specific magnitude range without basis — the correct answer is that the direction and magnitude of the true effect are unknown until a clean experiment runs. Option D raises the possibility of a negative true effect, which is possible but not the direct diagnosis of the described mechanism.
hints: The control arm has over-represented high-converting users (5.2% vs 2.8%). What does that do to the control arm's observed conversion rate relative to a balanced sample?
If the lift is primarily driven by user-composition differences, what happens to the lift estimate when the composition is equalized?

title: Q4 deadline in 3 weeks with asymmetric cost: design the most defensible experiment plan
scenario_context: Your team must test a new pricing algorithm before a Q4 deadline in 3 weeks. Standard fixed-horizon analysis requires 21 days (80% power, 2% MDE, α = 0.05). The business risk is asymmetric: shipping a bad pricing algorithm costs $2M in revenue loss. Missing a good one costs approximately $300K in forgone revenue. You have exactly 21 days.
description: Design the most defensible experiment plan given the deadline and asymmetric cost structure.
options: Run fixed-horizon for 21 days — sequential designs add complexity and the 21-day window exactly matches the required duration, providing no benefit over a standard fixed test.

Implement a group sequential design with O'Brien-Fleming alpha spending and 2 looks: look 1 at day 10 (early stop threshold z > 2.8, p < 0.005 — conservative because false-positive cost is 6.7× false-negative cost), final analysis at day 21 (z > 2.02, preserving most power). If the algorithm shows early harm, stop and avoid the $2M loss. If clearly beneficial, optionally stop. Otherwise, run to completion.
Run for 14 days with a one-tailed test — this halves the effective alpha and provides extra protection against a false positive on the pricing algorithm within a tighter timeline.
Run for 21 days with daily monitoring at α = 0.005 per look — this conservative per-look threshold keeps family-wise Type I error below 5% over 21 looks.
explanation: The group sequential design with OBF alpha spending provides two concrete benefits the fixed-horizon cannot: (1) an early stop at day 10 if the effect is clearly harmful (protecting against the $2M revenue risk — the primary asymmetric cost), and (2) a valid final analysis at day 21 with most of the original 80% power preserved. OBF's final-look threshold (z > 2.02) costs approximately 4 percentage points of power vs fixed-horizon — a small price for the early-harm-detection capability. The conservative early threshold (z > 2.8) is appropriate given that false positives cost 6.7× more than false negatives; the bar for early shipping should be very high. Option A ignores the harm-early-stop benefit — a fixed-horizon design requires waiting the full 21 days even if day-10 data clearly shows a negative effect. Option C (one-tailed, 14 days) changes the hypothesis structure and reduces duration without solving the early-harm-detection problem. Option D (daily monitoring at 0.005 per day) is not a valid sequential test — it doesn't correspond to a valid alpha spending function, and α = 0.005 × 21 > 0.05 in the worst case.
hints: If the pricing algorithm is clearly harmful at day 10, what is the benefit of pre-specified interim analysis vs running the full 21 days?
The asymmetric cost (false positive $2M, false negative $300K) — does this push toward a more or less conservative early-stop threshold?

title: Thompson Sampling bandit vs A/B for 3-variant test: what does the bandit optimize and sacrifice?
scenario_context: A team tests 3 homepage variants to maximize conversion rate. They propose Thompson Sampling bandit that dynamically allocates traffic based on real-time conversion estimates. An experimenter pushes back: 'Use a standard A/B test — bandits don't give you valid causal estimates.' The PM supports the bandit: 'We care about optimizing conversion during the experiment, not just learning.'
description: Evaluate both positions and identify what the bandit optimizes and what it sacrifices.
options: The experimenter is right — Thompson Sampling bandits always produce biased estimates and should never be used when causal learning is the goal.

Both positions are partially correct. The bandit optimizes cumulative reward during the experiment (less opportunity cost from showing inferior variants) but sacrifices statistical inference validity: as the bandit concentrates traffic on the apparent winner, losing variants receive decreasing sample, making their final estimates noisy and potentially biased. A standard A/B maintains equal allocation and produces unbiased estimates of all variants' effects, but incurs higher regret. The right choice depends on whether the team values maximum conversions during the test or reliable causal estimates of all variants for future decision-making.
The bandit is always better — it adapts to data and focuses sample on the winning variant, giving it more data and producing better estimates.
Use a Bayesian A/B test — this combines Bayesian posterior updates with fixed allocation, getting the benefits of both without the tradeoffs of a bandit.
explanation: Thompson Sampling balances exploration (learning variant quality) with exploitation (showing the apparent winner). As the bandit runs, traffic concentrates on the apparent winner, reducing sample to losing variants. This creates two inference problems: (1) losing variants' estimates become increasingly uncertain; (2) the allocation itself becomes correlated with the outcome — samples are no longer exchangeable, which can introduce selection bias in estimates. The bandit is good for scenarios where opportunity cost during the experiment is high and where you continuously deploy without a formal ship/no-ship decision. A standard A/B is good for getting unbiased estimates of all variants for future planning and for making a formal post-experiment causal claim. Option A overstates the case — bandits produce estimates, but those estimates are less precise for losing variants and causal validity depends on the allocation history. Option C is wrong: concentrating sample on the winner improves the winner's estimate but worsens the losers', which matters if you want to understand the full experiment. Option D (Bayesian A/B) is valid for learning but still uses fixed allocation and doesn't solve the regret problem.
hints: As the bandit concentrates traffic on the apparent winner, what happens to sample size (and estimate quality) for the losing variants?
What does the bandit optimize over the course of the experiment — cumulative reward or causal learning? Are these the same objective?

title: Leadership mandates stop-at-95% posterior: evaluate the policy and the Day 8 ship decision
scenario_context: Leadership sets a policy: all A/B tests use Bayesian analysis and ship when posterior P(improvement) > 95%. Week 1 results on a checkout algorithm: P(improvement) = 94.3%, posterior median = +1.4%, 95% CrI [−0.1%, +2.9%]. The team argues: 'Run one more day.' Day 8: P(improvement) = 95.2%. Leadership says ship.
description: Evaluate the policy and the specific Day 8 ship decision.
options: The policy is sound — Bayesian analysis with a pre-specified 95% threshold is a valid decision rule, and 95.2% at Day 8 clearly crosses it.

The policy has a hidden peeking problem: checking daily until 95% is crossed without a pre-specified maximum sample is equivalent to optional stopping. Even a Bayesian posterior can be exploited by continuous monitoring if the stopping rule is 'stop when threshold is crossed.' The 95% threshold is not equivalent to 5% Type I error control unless the stopping rule is pre-specified and the inference framework is anytime-valid. The 95% CrI barely excluding zero (lower bound −0.1% at Day 7) means practical significance is marginal.
The policy is wrong because Bayesian posteriors are subjective — the 95% figure depends on the prior, making it unsuitable for business decisions.
The policy is correct but the threshold should be 99%, not 95%, for decisions with financial impact.
explanation: The optional stopping problem applies to Bayesian analyses. For a true null effect, continuous monitoring of a Bayesian posterior will eventually cross 95% with non-trivial probability if monitored indefinitely — the probability of false crossing depends on the prior, monitoring frequency, and maximum sample. 'Stop when P(improvement) > 95%' without a pre-specified maximum sample or an anytime-valid inference framework is not equivalent to controlling the false-positive rate at 5%. The pattern here is particularly concerning: the team was at 94.3% and added one day to try to cross the threshold — this is the Bayesian equivalent of peeking. The 95% CrI barely excluding zero (lower bound −0.1%) means the practical effect is uncertain even if the threshold is crossed. The correct design: pre-specify a maximum sample and decision threshold before the experiment starts, or use an anytime-valid inference framework. Option A treats the threshold as automatically valid without questioning the stopping rule. Option C raises a legitimate concern about priors but mislabels Bayesian decisions as 'unsuitable' — explicit priors are a feature, not a flaw. Option D changes the threshold without addressing the optional stopping problem.
hints: Is 'stop when posterior P(improvement) > 95%' equivalent to controlling the false-positive rate at 5%? Under what conditions does it hold?
What is the Bayesian version of the peeking problem? Does the Bayesian framework automatically solve it?

title: Switchback experiment for ride-sharing driver pricing: design and interference
scenario_context: A ride-sharing platform tests surge pricing algorithm V2 on driver incentives. The platform has 50K active drivers and 500K daily rider sessions. Rider sessions and driver assignments are tightly coupled: a driver in treatment serves riders in both treatment and control zones. User-level randomization would contaminate rider experiences based on which driver they get.
description: Why is a switchback experiment appropriate here, and what design parameters matter most?
options: A switchback experiment is not needed — randomize drivers to treatment or control; rider experiences are independent of which driver they get.

A switchback experiment is appropriate because driver-rider coupling means user-level randomization violates SUTVA: treatment drivers affect riders across the network regardless of rider assignment. A switchback assigns the entire platform to V1 or V2 alternately across time periods, eliminating cross-arm contamination. Key design parameters: (1) period length must exceed carryover duration (how long driver behavior from the prior pricing regime persists), (2) sufficient period count for statistical power given between-period variance, (3) balanced timing across peak and off-peak hours to avoid confounding.
Use geo-cluster randomization instead of switchback — assign cities to V1 or V2 and compare. Switchback experiments have higher variance due to temporal confounds.
Randomize at the city level with a 24-hour washout between arms — this eliminates carryover without the complexity of switchback timing.
explanation: User-level or driver-level randomization fails on a marketplace with tight coupling: a driver assigned to V2 pricing adjusts routing and acceptance behavior in ways that affect all rider sessions they serve, regardless of those riders' assignment. SUTVA is violated because a rider's experience depends on the treatment assignment of their matched driver. A switchback experiment avoids this by randomizing across time rather than users: the entire platform operates under V1 or V2 in alternating periods, ensuring all interactions within a period are under the same pricing regime. Critical design parameters: period length must exceed carryover (if drivers take 30 minutes to adjust behavior after a pricing switch, the period must account for this); the number of periods determines effective sample size (not user count, but independent time periods); peak vs off-peak balance prevents confounding treatment with time-of-day effects. Option A incorrectly assumes driver-rider independence — in a marketplace, driver behavior (acceptance rates, routing) affects all riders they serve regardless of rider assignment. Option C (geo-cluster) is a valid alternative but creates market imbalances on a national platform. Option D (city-level with washout) is a form of geo-cluster randomization with the same market imbalance problem.
hints: If a treatment driver serves riders from both treatment and control groups, is that rider's experience independent of the driver's pricing assignment?
A switchback randomizes time periods, not users. What constitutes 'sufficient sample' — more users or more independent time periods?

title: National policy launch with no holdout: which quasi-experimental approach is most appropriate?
scenario_context: A fintech company launches a new fee structure nationally on March 1. There is no control group — all users are affected simultaneously. You want to estimate the causal effect on monthly transaction volume. You have 24 months of pre-launch data and 6 months of post-launch data. Competitor fintech companies did not change their fee structures.
description: Which quasi-experimental approach is most appropriate, and what assumptions must hold?
options: Use a pre-post comparison (post-launch average minus pre-launch average). This directly measures the change without needing a control group.

Difference-in-differences using competitor customers as a control group. Key assumption: in the absence of the fee change, your customers and competitor customers would have had the same transaction volume trend (parallel trends). Pre-period data can test trend stability, strengthening (but not proving) the assumption.

Interrupted time series (ITS) on your platform alone. Fit a trend model on the 24-month pre-period, project the counterfactual post-launch trend, and estimate the effect as the deviation from the projected trend.

Both DiD and ITS are valid with different assumptions — DiD is preferred when competitor trends are available and likely parallel; ITS is preferred when no control group is accessible. Neither is definitively superior without testing the assumptions against the data.
explanation: Both DiD and ITS are legitimate quasi-experimental approaches, and the choice depends on assumption plausibility. DiD requires the parallel trends assumption: your customers and competitor customers would have followed the same trend without the fee change. With 24 months of pre-data you can test pre-trend parallelism. Threat: competitor customers may differ in geography, demographics, or product usage in ways that cause divergent trends during the post-period. ITS uses only your platform's own historical trend as the counterfactual, avoiding assumptions about a different population. Threat: any concurrent event (macroeconomic shock, competitor campaign) that coincidentally changes at March 1 will confound the ITS estimate. Neither is unconditionally better. The best practice: run both and check consistency. If DiD and ITS estimates are close and their respective assumption tests pass, confidence is higher. Option A (pre-post) conflates time trends and seasonality with the treatment effect — the most biased of the three. Options B and C are each correct conditional on their assumptions holding, which is why Option D (acknowledging both) is the most defensible answer.
hints: Pre-post assumes no time trend. DiD assumes parallel trends with a control group. ITS assumes the pre-period trend extrapolates as the counterfactual. Which assumption is easiest to test with 24 months of pre-data?
If DiD and ITS give similar estimates, what does that suggest about the robustness of the causal claim?

title: 5% holdout for 12 months: holdout engagement declining — explain and assess bias direction
scenario_context: A team launches a new recommendation algorithm and keeps a 5% holdout group unexposed for 12 months. After month 3, holdout users' engagement is declining faster than treatment users. After month 6, holdout users show 8% lower session frequency than pre-launch baseline. The 12-month holdout analysis shows +11% session frequency lift for treatment vs holdout.
description: What is the most likely explanation for the holdout group's declining engagement, and what does it mean for the 12-month causal estimate?
options: The holdout group decline is expected — holdout users are not benefiting from improved recommendations, causing natural engagement drift. The +11% estimate is the correct causal effect.

The declining holdout engagement reflects holdout degradation bias: as the recommendation algorithm improves content discovery for 95% of users, the platform ecosystem evolves around the new system. Holdout users receive old-algorithm recommendations as the platform optimizes for treatment users — their experience degrades relative to the platform's actual trajectory. This inflates the holdout-vs-treatment gap, causing the +11% estimate to overstate the true causal effect of the algorithm.
The holdout engagement decline is a seasonality artifact — months 3–6 post-launch coincide with a seasonal period when engagement typically drops. This is unrelated to the experiment.
The holdout decline is caused by selection bias: the 5% holdout selection over-represents low-engagement users who would have declined anyway.
explanation: Long-running holdout groups in recommendation system experiments suffer from holdout degradation bias: the holdout is not held against a static counterfactual but against a platform actively evolving around the treatment. As the algorithm improves content discovery and engagement for 95% of users, the platform ecosystem changes: content creation may shift toward formats that perform well in the new algorithm; social interactions increase among treatment users; the overall platform quality degrades from the holdout user's perspective (who receives old recommendations in a platform optimized for new-algorithm content). This makes the holdout's experience deteriorate over time — not because the old system is bad in isolation but because the platform evolves away from it. The measured treatment effect (treatment engagement minus holdout engagement) becomes upwardly biased as the holdout baseline degrades. Option A correctly identifies that holdout users miss improvements but doesn't recognize this as creating upward bias in the estimate. Option C (seasonality) is possible but contradicted by the holdout declining relative to its own pre-launch baseline, not just relative to treatment. Option D (selection bias) is contradicted by the randomized 5% holdout selection from launch day 1.
hints: If the recommendation algorithm is improving content discovery for 95% of users, how does that change the platform ecosystem for the 5% in the holdout?
If the holdout group's experience is actively degrading (not just failing to improve), does that make the treatment-vs-holdout gap larger or smaller than the true causal effect?

title: HTE: −2% mobile, +8% desktop. PM wants to ship to desktop only — evaluate the risks
scenario_context: A search redesign experiment shows overall: +5.1% lift (p = 0.001). Segment analysis (post-hoc, unplanned): desktop (40% of users): +8.3% lift (p = 0.0003). Mobile (60% of users): −2.1% lift (p = 0.12). The PM wants to ship to desktop only and continue testing on mobile.
description: What are the statistical and operational risks of shipping to desktop only based on this HTE analysis?
options: Ship to desktop only — p = 0.0003 is very strong evidence, and the non-significant mobile result means there is no evidence of harm. Selective deployment is the right call.

Shipping to desktop only based on an unplanned HTE carries two risks: (1) the HTE finding needs multiple-testing correction (Bonferroni for 2 segments gives threshold 0.025; desktop p = 0.0003 clears this, but the decision was informed by seeing both segment results); (2) the mobile −2.1% (p = 0.12) is non-significant but the CI likely includes meaningfully negative values. Selective deployment creates platform inconsistency for cross-device users and warrants a focused mobile follow-up before dismissing the negative signal.
Do not ship at all — the mobile negative effect must be resolved before any deployment, even to desktop.
Ship to all users — the overall +5.1% is significant and the HTE reflects known measurement noise. The overall estimate is the reliable one.
explanation: Selective deployment based on an unplanned HTE finding requires careful handling. The desktop effect (p = 0.0003) does clear a Bonferroni correction for 2 segments (threshold 0.025), so statistical evidence for a desktop positive effect is real. However: (1) HTE findings are notoriously sample-sensitive — the interaction (desktop vs mobile differential) needs its own power calculation; the observed −2.1% on mobile could be noise or a real harm. (2) Selective desktop deployment has operational consequences: cross-device users see inconsistent experiences; the mobile redesign must eventually be resolved. (3) Non-significant ≠ no effect: the mobile CI likely includes meaningfully negative values given the 60% mobile share. The defensible action: ship to desktop (strong evidence), run a focused mobile-specific follow-up experiment to confirm or refute the negative trend. Option A dismisses the mobile signal too quickly on 'non-significant' grounds. Option C is overly conservative — the desktop evidence is strong. Option D ignores the HTE by relying solely on the overall estimate, masking a potentially harmful mobile effect.
hints: The mobile result (−2.1%, p = 0.12) is non-significant. Does non-significant mean there is no harm? What does the 90% CI on the mobile segment likely include?
A cross-device user under desktop-only deployment: what do they experience? Is the platform experience consistent?

title: Email sharing feature: 30% control users clicked referral links — does +3.8% over- or under-estimate?
scenario_context: A team tests a new email-sharing feature. 30% of control users received referral links from treatment users and clicked through. Control users who received links have 11% higher 30-day retention than control non-link-recipients. Measured treatment-vs-control lift: +3.8% retention (p = 0.024).
description: Explain the SUTVA violation and assess whether +3.8% over- or under-estimates the true causal effect.
options: The +3.8% overestimates the true effect — referral links contaminate control users positively, raising their retention and narrowing the true treatment-control gap.

The +3.8% underestimates the true effect. Referral links elevate control users' retention (11% higher among link-recipients vs non-recipients), raising the control arm's average retention above a clean counterfactual (no-feature world). The measured gap (treatment minus inflated control) is smaller than the true causal effect of fully deploying the feature.
The +3.8% is unbiased — referral-link exposure is correlated with high engagement, not caused by the treatment. High-engagement control users were going to be retained regardless.
The bias direction is indeterminate without knowing the counterfactual retention rate of control users without any referral links.
explanation: Referral links from treatment users deliver a measurable benefit to the control users who receive them (11% higher retention among link-recipients). These control users have been partially treated — they've engaged with the feature's output (the shared email content), even without access to the active feature. This inflates the control arm's retention above what it would be in a true no-feature world. The measured treatment effect (treatment retention − inflated control retention) is narrowed below the true causal effect of fully deploying the feature. In a fully deployed world, even more referral links would circulate (from the new treatment users), compounding the retention benefit. The +3.8% is a lower bound on the true causal effect. Option A inverts the direction: referral links raise control retention (making control look better), which narrows the gap — the estimate is smaller, not larger, than the true effect. Option C attributes the elevated retention to pre-existing engagement: even if this is true, the directional impact on the estimate is the same — if link-recipients are higher-engagement regardless, removing them from the control group would lower the control baseline, widening the gap further. Option D defers when the direction is determinable from the mechanism.
hints: Control users who received referral links have 11% higher retention. How does this affect the control arm's average retention relative to a clean control?
If the control arm's retention is artificially elevated by spillover, is the measured treatment-control gap larger or smaller than the true causal effect?

title: MDE = 0.5% needs 4M per arm; PM has 200K DAU for 2 weeks — what are the honest options?
scenario_context: Your power analysis requires 4,047,000 users per arm to detect 0.5% relative lift (10% conversion rate, σ = 30%, 80% power, α = 0.05). The PM has 200K DAU and a 2-week constraint. CUPED reduces variance by 35%. At 100K per arm per day, 2 weeks gives 1.4M per arm.
description: What is the honest set of options, and which tradeoff must the PM accept?
options: Run for 2 weeks at α = 0.10 instead of 0.05 — loosening the threshold reduces required sample by ~15%, partially closing the gap.

With CUPED (35% variance reduction), required n drops to ~2.63M per arm (not 1.4M). At 100K per arm per day, that requires ~26 days — still outside the 2-week constraint. The honest options: (A) Widen the MDE to ~2.5% — required n drops to ~105K per arm after CUPED, achievable in ~1 day; or (B) Accept ~42% power at 0.5% MDE with CUPED in the 2-week window — valid but under-powered. The PM must choose between a wider MDE target or drastically lower power.
Apply CUPED (35% variance reduction) and run 2 weeks — this gives approximately 60% power at 0.5% MDE, which is acceptable for a business decision.
Extend the experiment to 40 days — CUPED reduces required sample to 2.63M per arm, achievable in ~27 days at 100K per arm per day.
explanation: After CUPED: required n = 4,047,000 × 0.65 ≈ 2,630,000 per arm. At 100K per arm per day: 2,630,000 / 100,000 = 26.3 days needed — still 12 days beyond the constraint. At the 2-week window: 1.4M per arm. Power at 0.5% MDE with variance-reduced σ ≈ 24.5% and n = 1.4M: approximately 42–45%, not 60%. For MDE widening: at 2.5% MDE, required n = 4,047,000 × (0.5/2.5)² × 0.65 = 4,047,000 × 0.04 × 0.65 ≈ 105K per arm — achievable in ~1 day. The PM has only two real options: (1) widen the MDE substantially (0.5% → 2.5%) and get a valid 2-week result, or (2) accept ~42% power (not 60%) for the original 0.5% MDE. Option A (widen α to 0.10) reduces required n by ~15% — from 2.63M to ~2.23M per arm — still 10× too large for 2 weeks. Option C claims 60% power at 2 weeks with CUPED — the actual power is ~42%, not 60%. Option D correctly identifies the needed duration (~27 days) but ignores the PM's 2-week constraint and doesn't give the PM the tradeoff options.
hints: After a 35% variance reduction from pre-experiment covariates, what is the new required n per arm? At 100K per arm per day, how many days does that take?
At 1.4M per arm (2-week constraint) and variance-reduced σ ≈ 24.5%, what power do you actually achieve at 0.5% MDE? Is it 60%?

title: Post-fix investigation reveals bot traffic imbalance — what does this mean for your SRM?
scenario_context: After fixing the CDN routing bug (from the previous question), you investigate the assignment logs and discover that before the fix, 62% of bot traffic was landing in treatment and 38% in control. Human user splits remain close to 50/50 throughout. Your product metric (checkout conversion) is near-zero for bots. The PM argues: 'Bots don't convert, so they can't affect conversion rate — the lift is still valid.'
description: Is the PM's reasoning correct?
options: The PM is wrong. Even if bots have near-zero conversion, imbalanced bot counts inflate the denominator in one arm asymmetrically. If bots crowd out human impressions in the treatment arm (e.g., through session slots or logging), the human sample composition may differ. The conversion rate denominator is biased, invalidating the lift estimate even if bots themselves do not convert.

The PM is correct. Bots have ~0 conversion rate, so they add noise equally to numerator (0 conversions) and denominator. The conversion rate for human users is unaffected and the lift remains a valid causal estimate.
The PM is correct for the primary metric (conversion) but wrong for secondary metrics like page load time, where bot behavior would directly inflate the treatment arm's average.
The PM is wrong because bot sessions always convert at a non-zero rate due to automated form submissions; the numerator is inflated in treatment.
explanation: Option A is correct. The PM's reasoning fails because 'bots don't convert' does not mean they are benign for the analysis. Imbalanced bots change the denominator of the conversion rate in each arm. If the treatment arm has proportionally more bot sessions, it has proportionally fewer human sessions per unit of exposure — meaning the treatment sample is drawn from a different pool of human users than the control sample. Even if every bot produces 0 conversions, the human-to-bot ratio determines how representative the human subsample is. Option B assumes bots are additive noise but ignores the denominator bias in session-based metrics. Option C is a partial truth that misses the denominator problem for conversion. Option D introduces an unsupported claim about bot conversion rates.
hints: Focus on what the denominator of your conversion rate represents.
If the treatment arm has more bots, what fraction of its sessions are human?

title: PM wants to ship based on biased SRM window — how do you respond?
scenario_context: The CDN routing bug ran for days 1–4 of your 14-day experiment. Days 5–14 show a clean 50/50 split. The PM proposes: 'Let's just use days 5–14 data — that's 10 clean days, plenty of sample. The lift is still +3.2% (p=0.04) on those days. Ship it.' You have 180K sessions in the clean window (90K per arm).
description: What is your recommendation?
options: Agree — the 10-day clean window is a valid post-hoc experiment; the SRM only affected days 1–4, which are now excluded, and the p-value is below 0.05.

Reject the ship recommendation. The clean-window analysis is a post-hoc slice that was not pre-specified; the decision to cut at day 5 was made after seeing the split, introducing selection bias. Additionally, novelty effects and week-of-week seasonality are not controlled in a 10-day slice that starts mid-week. Restart with a fresh pre-specified experiment.
Accept the analysis but widen the confidence interval by a Bonferroni factor of 2 to account for the multiple looks (dirty window vs. clean window), then ship if still significant.
Use the full 14-day window but reweight days 1–4 to match the 50/50 expected split using inverse-probability weighting, then ship if lift holds.
explanation: Option B is correct. Post-hoc window selection is a form of data dredging: the cut point (day 5) was chosen after observing the data pattern, not pre-specified in the analysis plan. The resulting estimate has unknown bias from the selection process itself (we might have chosen a different cut if the SRM had lasted 7 days). Additionally, a mid-experiment fresh start is not the same randomized sample as a pre-specified experiment — day 5 onward users are already post-exposure to the broken assignment period. Option A treats a post-hoc decision as if it were a clean RCT. Option C applies Bonferroni to the wrong problem (multiple comparisons, not selection bias). Option D is an interesting reweighting idea but it corrects days 1–4 without addressing the post-hoc selection problem and introduces IPW complexity that still cannot fix the non-pre-specified cut.
hints: What makes a post-hoc window selection different from a pre-specified analysis?
Who chose day 5 as the cut point, and when was that decision made?

title: 6-hour tracking gap at look 1 — does it invalidate the sequential boundary?
scenario_context: Your mSPRT sequential test has three pre-planned looks: day 7, day 14, and day 21. During look 1 (day 7), you discover a 6-hour logging outage that equally affected both treatment and control arms (confirmed via assignment logs: 4,812 events dropped in control, 4,798 in treatment — within 0.3% of each other). Server-side hour-by-hour event counts confirm the outage was distributed roughly uniformly across its 6-hour window (02:00–08:00 UTC), not concentrated in peak shopping hours, and the conversion rate in the affected window matches the surrounding 24-hour baseline within normal variance. The look-1 statistic is below the stopping boundary, so you did not stop. The gap represents about 4% of day-7 observations.
description: How should you handle the tracking gap for the remainder of the sequential analysis?
options: The symmetric gap (both arms equally affected, <0.3% imbalance) means the conversion rate comparison is unbiased for the affected window. Document the outage, note it in the analysis, and continue the sequential test without modification — the boundary calibration is robust to small symmetric noise of this magnitude.

A symmetric gap in session count does not guarantee an unbiased conversion rate comparison — high-intent users may convert at different rates depending on when events are lost. If the outage hit peak shopping hours, the missing events could be non-randomly distributed within the funnel. You must assess the gap's timing against hourly conversion patterns before concluding neutrality.
Exclude all of day 7 from both arms and recompute the sequential boundary from scratch using only days 8–21 as the new horizon — this removes the contaminated period cleanly.
The gap invalidates the sequential analysis because mSPRT requires uninterrupted data collection to maintain the always-valid guarantee; restart the experiment from day 1.
explanation: Option A is correct for this scenario. The gap is symmetric (both arms affected proportionally, <0.3% imbalance), small (4% of day-7 data), and the look-1 statistic did not trigger stopping. mSPRT's anytime-valid property is robust to small symmetric data-quality noise — the always-valid guarantee is about Type I error control across the martingale, not about requiring every observation. Documenting the gap and continuing is the operationally sound call. Option B raises a valid concern in principle (peak-hour selection bias), but the scenario provides hour-by-hour event counts confirming the outage was uniformly distributed outside peak hours and that conversion rates in the affected window matched the surrounding baseline. With that evidence in hand, B's concern is addressed — continuing without modification is the sound call. Option C discards clean data unnecessarily and rebasing the horizon changes the preplanned look schedule, which introduces its own multiple-testing complexity. Option D overstates the fragility of mSPRT — restarting wastes 7 days of valid data for a 4% symmetric gap.
hints: What does 'symmetric gap' mean for the treatment-control comparison?
Does mSPRT's always-valid guarantee require zero missing data, or tolerance for small symmetric noise?

title: Business changes primary metric mid-sequential experiment — what now?
scenario_context: You are at look 2 (day 14) of your 3-look mSPRT sequential test, originally powered on checkout conversion rate. The business has just rebranded its Q4 goal from 'checkout conversion' to 'revenue per session' (RPS) as the primary success metric. The VP of Product says: 'Just rerun the sequential analysis on RPS — the experiment is the same, just the metric changed.' Look-2 data is already collected.
description: What is the right response to the VP's request?
options: Refuse to rerun on RPS as the primary metric. The mSPRT boundary was calibrated for checkout conversion variance; applying it to RPS (a higher-variance, skewed metric) with data already collected is a post-hoc metric swap that inflates Type I error. Report the current conversion result as the pre-specified primary outcome and treat RPS as an exploratory secondary.
Rerun the sequential analysis on RPS — the experiment design (randomization, duration, look schedule) is unchanged; only the metric changed, which does not affect the boundary validity.
Restart the experiment from scratch with RPS as the primary metric and a freshly calibrated mSPRT boundary — the current data cannot be used for any inference on RPS.
Apply a Bonferroni correction dividing alpha by 2 (one for conversion, one for RPS) and rerun the sequential test on both; ship if either metric is significant.
explanation: Option A is correct. Switching the primary metric mid-experiment after observing data is a form of p-hacking / HARKing (Hypothesizing After Results are Known). The mSPRT boundary was calibrated for the variance profile of checkout conversion; RPS is a skewed, higher-variance metric where the boundary may be miscalibrated. More fundamentally, if the business is now looking at RPS because conversion results were disappointing, the metric swap is outcome-driven — exactly the selection bias that Type I error control is designed to prevent. The pre-specified analysis plan (conversion) must be reported as the primary outcome. RPS can be reported as exploratory with appropriate caveats. Option B incorrectly asserts that boundary validity is independent of metric variance. Option C is overly conservative — the collected data is valid for the pre-specified primary metric. Option D applies Bonferroni to a problem of post-hoc selection, not planned multiple comparisons.
hints: Was the decision to switch to RPS made before or after seeing the look-2 conversion result?
What happens to Type I error control when you swap the metric the boundary was calibrated for?

title: Thompson Sampling routes only 3% to variant C after 7 days — is this a problem?
scenario_context: Your Thompson Sampling bandit (from the previous question) has been running for 7 days across three variants (A, B, C). Traffic allocation has stabilized: A=48%, B=49%, C=3%. Variant C is a bold redesign your design team spent 3 months on. The design team lead argues: 'The bandit killed C unfairly — it got much less data early and was never given a fair chance. We should reset the priors and give C a 33%/33%/33% fresh start.'
description: How do you respond to the design team lead?
options: Reject the reset request. The bandit allocating 3% to C is the algorithm working correctly — C performed poorly on early observations and the bandit reduced its allocation to protect users. Resetting to uniform priors discards 7 days of signal and restarts the exploration-exploitation tradeoff from scratch, likely repeating the same allocation outcome if C's underlying performance is genuinely weak.
Agree with the reset. Thompson Sampling is known to be sensitive to early outcomes and C may have received bad luck in the first few days; a uniform restart gives it a fair trial.
Agree with the reset but run C as a separate A/B test against A (the current winner) rather than a 3-variant bandit, to give it a statistically clean comparison.
Keep the current allocation but manually boost C to 15% traffic by overriding the bandit, then let the algorithm rebalance from that floor.
explanation: Option A is correct. Thompson Sampling's allocation is Bayesian posterior-based: C receiving 3% reflects the evidence accumulated over 7 days, not arbitrary bad luck. Resetting priors discards that evidence — it is analytically equivalent to saying 'ignore the last 7 days of data,' which the design team would not accept for any other reason. If C is genuinely underperforming, a reset will re-route users to a worse variant during the re-exploration phase. The right response is to examine C's posterior distribution: if its 95% credible interval still overlaps A and B, it has not been statistically eliminated and exploration will continue. If it has been dominated, the bandit's conclusion is correct. Option B conflates 'the algorithm gave bad luck' with 'the algorithm gave a bad outcome' — Thompson Sampling is robust to early-arm variance by design. Option C introduces a new experiment design mid-stream. Option D manually overrides the algorithm's posterior-based allocation, which negates the bandit's function.
hints: What does a 3% allocation mean in a Bayesian bandit's posterior framework?
What is the difference between 'C got unlucky' and 'C performed poorly'?

title: Reward for Thompson Sampling is observed 24 hours after exposure — what is the design implication?
scenario_context: Your e-commerce bandit tests checkout-flow variants against a 7-day repeat-purchase rate (the business's key loyalty metric). The reward signal (did the user repurchase within 7 days?) arrives 7 days after the visit. Thompson Sampling updates its posteriors on each new reward observation. The engineering team proposes: 'We'll just wait 7 days per batch before updating the bandit — that limits us to one posterior update per week.'
description: What is the core design tension this delayed reward creates, and how should it be resolved?
options: Delayed rewards create a feedback lag that decouples the bandit's posterior from current user behavior. Weekly batch updates are operationally safe but sacrifice most of the bandit's regret advantage — it is nearly equivalent to a fixed-allocation A/B test with weekly looks. Consider a short-horizon surrogate metric (e.g., add-to-cart or same-session purchase) to update posteriors in near-real-time, validated against 7-day repeat purchase in a holdout.
The 7-day delay is not a design problem — Thompson Sampling does not require real-time updates. Batch updates every 7 days are standard and fully preserve the Bayesian regret guarantees.
The delay means the bandit cannot be used at all for 7-day metrics; switch to a fixed A/B test with 7-day conversion as the primary endpoint.
Run two bandits in parallel: one on a 1-day surrogate metric and one on the 7-day metric, then combine their allocations using a weighted average of the two posteriors.
explanation: Option A is correct. The bandit's regret advantage over a fixed A/B test comes from its ability to shift traffic quickly toward better-performing arms. A 7-day reward lag plus weekly posterior updates means the bandit is essentially making decisions based on week-old evidence — if one variant spikes or tanks in the current week, the bandit cannot respond for 7 more days. This erases the adaptive advantage. The surrogate-metric approach (near-real-time proxy for the eventual 7-day metric) is the standard solution in e-commerce bandit design. Option B is wrong: batch updates do not fully preserve regret guarantees when the lag is as long as the update interval — the regret bound degrades significantly with feedback delay. Option C overstates the limitation; bandits with delayed rewards are used in practice, just with careful design choices. Option D is an interesting idea but combining posteriors from different metrics with a 'weighted average' is not statistically principled and conflates two different optimization targets.
hints: What is the bandit's main advantage over a fixed A/B test, and what does feedback lag do to that advantage?
What is a surrogate metric, and why is it used in delayed-reward bandit settings?

title: Board asks: 'What is our confidence level?' — how do you translate the Bayesian result?
scenario_context: You stopped your Bayesian experiment at 95% posterior probability that treatment beats control (P(treatment > control) = 0.951). The board is presenting to investors and asks: 'Can we say we are 95.1% confident the new checkout flow is better?' You know the board will quote this number publicly.
description: What is the correct response?
options: Correct the framing before it goes public. '95.1% posterior probability' is a Bayesian statement about the parameter given your prior and data — it is not a frequentist confidence level and should not be quoted as generic 'confidence.' For investor communication, say: 'Our Bayesian analysis gives a 95.1% posterior probability that the new checkout flow has a higher conversion rate, under our stated prior assumptions.' Omitting the prior dependency is misleading.
The statement is accurate as-is. Bayesian posterior probability is the most intuitive form of confidence and the board can quote it directly.
Do not allow the board to quote any Bayesian result to investors — Bayesian statistics are not accepted in regulated financial disclosures and create legal liability.
Convert the posterior probability to a frequentist p-value before communicating — p = 1 - 0.951 = 0.049 — and quote that instead, as it is more universally understood.
explanation: Option A is correct. The Bayesian posterior probability is a conditional statement: P(treatment > control | data, prior). The prior dependency is not a technicality — it is load-bearing. If the prior was informative (e.g., you assumed a 50% chance of a positive effect with a specific effect-size distribution), the 95.1% figure reflects that assumption. Public statements that strip the prior condition mislead audiences into treating it as an unconditional probability. The correction is not to avoid Bayesian results but to communicate them with their conditioning clearly stated. Option B ignores the prior dependency. Option C is false — Bayesian methods are widely used in regulated industries with appropriate disclosure. Option D is statistically wrong: p = 1 - posterior_probability only if the prior was uniform and the test was two-sided, which is generally not the case; conflating the two frameworks produces an invalid hybrid.
hints: What is the full conditioning statement for a Bayesian posterior probability?
Does '95.1% posterior probability' depend on the prior? What happens if the prior was wrong?

title: Leadership changes success metric to revenue after Bayesian experiment stopped on conversion
scenario_context: You stopped your Bayesian experiment at P(treatment > control on conversion rate) = 0.951. Leadership now says: 'Conversion is fine, but we really care about revenue per user. Can you rerun the same Bayesian analysis on revenue?' Revenue per user in your data is highly right-skewed (median: $12, mean: $34, 90th percentile: $180). You have 85,000 users per arm.
description: What are the two distinct problems with running a Bayesian analysis on revenue using the already-collected data?
options: Problem 1: Post-hoc metric selection. The decision to analyze revenue was made after seeing the conversion result, introducing the same selection bias as frequentist p-hacking — you are choosing the metric most likely to support a ship decision. Problem 2: Distributional mismatch. Revenue is highly right-skewed; a standard Bayesian model with a conjugate beta-binomial prior (designed for conversion rates) is the wrong likelihood, and the posterior will be miscalibrated. Both problems compound to produce an untrustworthy result.

There is only one problem: the distributional mismatch (revenue is skewed). Use a log-normal Bayesian model instead of beta-binomial, rerun the analysis, and report the posterior on revenue — there is no post-hoc selection issue because Bayesian inference does not have a Type I error problem.
There are no problems. Bayesian analysis on the same dataset with a different metric is always valid because Bayesian posteriors are not affected by multiple comparisons.

The only problem is sample size: 85,000 per arm is sufficient for conversion but may be underpowered for the higher-variance revenue metric. Compute the posterior probability on revenue and report it with a wider credible interval.
explanation: Option A is correct on both counts. (1) Post-hoc metric selection: the Bayesian framework does not eliminate selection bias. If you choose to analyze revenue because conversion was significant (or because you hope revenue will be significant), you are fishing for a favorable result. The prior and likelihood are chosen after seeing what was available — this is HARKing regardless of the inference framework. (2) Distributional mismatch: a beta-binomial model is parameterized for binary outcomes (converted / did not convert). Revenue is continuous and highly skewed; a log-normal, gamma, or mixture model is needed. Using the wrong likelihood produces posteriors that do not reflect the true parameter distribution. Option B correctly identifies the distributional problem but incorrectly claims Bayesian inference is immune to selection bias. Option C is a common misconception: multiple comparison protection is a frequentist concept, but post-hoc selection bias affects all inference frameworks. Option D only addresses power, missing both the selection and distributional problems.
hints: Does the Bayesian framework protect against choosing your metric after seeing the data?
What likelihood function is appropriate for a right-skewed revenue distribution?

title: Switchback shows 45-minute carryover into a 1-hour period — is the design valid?
scenario_context: Your switchback experiment uses 1-hour time periods, alternating between control and treatment surge pricing. Analysis of driver repositioning behavior reveals a 45-minute carryover effect: after a period ends, driver positions influenced by the previous period's pricing persist for ~45 minutes into the next period. Your switchback design assumed 15-minute carryover when setting the 1-hour period length.
description: What does the 45-minute carryover mean for your experiment's validity?
options: The design is severely compromised. With 45-minute carryover in a 1-hour period, only ~15 minutes of each period reflects 'pure' treatment or control conditions. Observations in the first 45 minutes of each period are contaminated by the previous period's pricing. The causal estimate from this design conflates the previous period's effect with the current period's effect, biasing the result in an unknown direction. The experiment must be redesigned with longer periods (e.g., 3–4 hours) or a washout gap between periods.

The carryover is a minor issue. The 45-minute effect only affects the first 45 minutes of each period; since the period is 60 minutes, 75% of observations are clean. Average the last 15 minutes of each period and ignore the first 45.

Carryover effects cancel out in expectation in a switchback design because treatment and control alternate — what bleeds from treatment into control also bleeds from control into treatment symmetrically.
Extend each period to 90 minutes without changing the alternation schedule — this gives more time per period for the carryover to dissipate before the next switch.
explanation: Option A is correct. The carryover/washout assumption is foundational to switchback validity. If carryover is 45 minutes and the period is 60 minutes, only 15 minutes of 'pure signal' exists per period — and only if the carryover is exactly 45 minutes (not longer). The estimate computed from full-period data is a weighted mix of the current and previous treatments, not a clean causal estimate of the current treatment alone. Option B's suggestion to use only the last 15 minutes dramatically reduces power (one-quarter of the data) and may still be contaminated if the carryover estimate of 45 minutes is itself noisy. Option C is wrong: carryover effects do not cancel in a switchback — they systematically contaminate the early portion of every period regardless of direction. Option D is on the right track (longer periods) but 90 minutes still barely exceeds the 45-minute carryover, leaving an insufficient washout margin; the standard recommendation is 3–4× the estimated carryover.
hints: What fraction of each period is 'pure signal' when carryover is 45 minutes and the period is 60 minutes?
Do carryover effects cancel when you alternate treatment and control?

title: Expanding switchback to 3 new markets mid-experiment — what's the risk?
scenario_context: Your ride-sharing switchback experiment has been running in New York for 3 weeks. Leadership asks you to expand to Chicago and Los Angeles mid-experiment to 'get results faster.' The new markets would be added to the existing switchback schedule starting in week 4. Supply elasticity, driver density, and surge pricing response rates differ substantially across the three cities.
description: What is the primary experimental validity concern with mid-experiment market expansion?
options: Adding markets mid-experiment introduces heterogeneous treatment effects across markets that were not present in the original design, confounding city-level differences with the treatment effect. If Chicago and LA have different supply elasticity, their causal response to surge pricing cannot be pooled with New York's without a market fixed effect. More critically, the week 4 addition creates a non-random time-market interaction: New York has 3 weeks of data while new markets have 1 week, making the pooled estimate sensitive to time-varying confounders in weeks 1–3.
Mid-experiment market expansion is standard in switchback designs — more markets increase statistical power. Add the markets and pool all data from week 1 onward for Chicago and LA.

The primary concern is timezone differences: since switchbacks alternate by hour, Chicago (CT) and LA (PT) periods do not align with New York (ET), causing the alternation schedule to be desynchronized.
Expanding markets mid-experiment is fine as long as you use clustered standard errors at the market-period level to account for within-market correlation.
explanation: Option A is correct. Mid-experiment expansion has two compounding problems. First, heterogeneous treatment effects: if the causal effect of surge pricing on driver supply differs by city (plausible given different driver density and market maturity), pooling creates a mixture estimate that is not generalizable to any single market. Second, the time-market confound: New York has 3 weeks of data including any early novelty effects; Chicago and LA start in week 4 under potentially different market conditions (season, local events, competitor changes). This creates a spurious correlation between market identity and experiment phase. Options 2 and 4 address the right direction (power, variance structure) but ignore the selection confound from non-random market timing. Option D identifies a real operational challenge (timezone alignment) but it is secondary to the confounding concern.
hints: If NYC has 3 weeks and Chicago has 1 week of data, what time-varying factors might differ?
Can you pool causal estimates across cities with different supply elasticities without accounting for those differences?

title: DiD and interrupted time series disagree by 3pp — which do you trust?
scenario_context: Your national policy rollout used two quasi-experimental methods: (1) Difference-in-Differences (DiD) comparing early-adopter regions vs. late-adopter regions before and after rollout, yielding a +5.2% estimated effect. (2) Interrupted Time Series (ITS) on the early-adopter regions alone, using pre-rollout trend extrapolation, yielding a +8.1% estimated effect. The disagreement is 2.9 percentage points.
description: What does the disagreement between DiD and ITS tell you, and which estimate should you report?
options: The disagreement is diagnostic, not a problem to resolve by picking a winner. DiD assumes parallel trends between early and late adopters (any violation biases it); ITS assumes the pre-rollout trend would have continued unchanged (any structural break biases it). A 2.9pp gap suggests at least one assumption is violated. Investigate: (a) test the parallel-trends assumption using pre-period data, (b) check for confounding events near rollout that ITS's counterfactual trend would miss. Report both estimates with their assumption dependencies and flag the disagreement as uncertainty.
Trust DiD because it uses a control group (late adopters), making it more robust than ITS which relies only on trend extrapolation.
Trust ITS because it uses only early-adopter data, avoiding any contamination from the late-adopter group's behavior near the rollout date.
Average the two estimates (+6.65%) and report that as the consensus effect — this hedges against the failure of either single assumption.
explanation: Option A is correct.
