When two valid quasi-experimental methods disagree, the disagreement is evidence that at least one identifying assumption is violated — it is not resolved by picking the 'better' method a priori. DiD's parallel-trends assumption can be tested empirically using pre-period trend data (if early and late adopters diverged before the policy, the assumption fails). ITS's counterfactual-trend assumption is violated when there are contemporaneous shocks (macro events, competitor changes, seasonality shifts near rollout). The right response is to surface both estimates with their conditioning assumptions and explain what the gap implies. Option B correctly notes DiD's control-group advantage but incorrectly dismisses ITS; DiD is not universally better and can fail on parallel trends. Option C is the reverse error. Option D averaging arbitrary estimators is not statistically principled — averaging a biased and an unbiased estimate produces a biased result.
hints: What assumption does DiD require that ITS does not? What assumption does ITS require that DiD does not?
When two methods disagree, what does that disagreement tell you about their assumptions?

title: Business wants a 95% CI on a quasi-experimental effect — can you provide one?
scenario_context: After your DiD analysis (from the previous question), the finance team asks for a 95% confidence interval on the +5.2% policy effect for their revenue forecast model. They want to use the CI bounds as the pessimistic and optimistic inputs. Your DiD standard errors come from a standard OLS regression with region-clustered standard errors (12 regions, 24 months of data).
description: What is the correct response to the finance team's request?
options: Provide the CI with explicit caveats. The statistical CI from your OLS regression quantifies sampling uncertainty (noise around the point estimate given the model), but it does NOT capture assumption uncertainty — specifically, the risk that parallel trends is violated. If parallel trends fails, the entire +5.2% estimate is biased and the CI interval around a biased estimate is also biased. Communicate: 'The statistical CI is [X%, Y%], but this interval conditions on the parallel trends assumption being valid. Our assumption-violation risk (evidenced by the DiD/ITS disagreement) is not captured in these bounds.'
Do not provide a CI for quasi-experimental estimates — confidence intervals require random sampling and quasi-experimental designs are not randomized, so standard error computations are invalid.
Provide the CI as-is from the OLS regression. Standard errors with region clustering are the appropriate measure of uncertainty for DiD, and the finance team can use the bounds directly.
Widen the CI manually by a factor of 2 to account for assumption uncertainty, then provide it to the finance team as a conservative interval.
explanation: Option A is correct. A CI from OLS regression captures one type of uncertainty: sampling variability around the point estimate, conditional on the model being correctly specified. It does not capture assumption uncertainty — the risk that parallel trends is violated, that the treatment timing is endogenous, or that there is an omitted variable. In a setting where DiD and ITS already disagree by 2.9pp (from the previous question), assumption uncertainty is real and material. Communicating the CI without this caveat leads the finance team to treat the bounds as capturing all relevant uncertainty, which they do not. Option B is incorrect: frequentist standard errors are applicable to regression on observational data — the issue is not about random sampling but about model assumptions. Option C provides the CI without the critical caveat about assumption uncertainty. Option D's arbitrary 2× widening has no principled basis — it is better than providing no caveat but worse than explaining what the CI actually measures.
hints: What does a confidence interval from OLS regression measure? What does it not measure?
If parallel trends is violated, what happens to the point estimate that the CI is centered on?

title: Holdout tracking shows 2% measurement gap in long-run holdout — how does this affect the estimate?
scenario_context: Your 12-month holdout (5% of users withheld from all feature launches) shows a +3.8% cumulative revenue lift for the treated group vs. holdout after 12 months. A data audit reveals that 2% of holdout users were accidentally enrolled in a feature during month 7 (a logging bug briefly assigned them treatment). The 2% contamination received the feature for approximately 3 weeks before being re-assigned to holdout.
description: What is the impact of the contamination on your holdout estimate?
options: The contamination introduces treatment spillover into the holdout arm, causing the estimated lift to be understated. If 2% of 'holdout' users actually received treatment for 3 weeks, the holdout arm's revenue is slightly inflated relative to a pure holdout, compressing the treatment-holdout gap. The true long-run lift is likely larger than +3.8%. The magnitude of the bias depends on how much of the long-run effect accrued during those 3 weeks.
The contamination inflates the estimated lift. The 2% of holdout users who received the feature behaved better than pure holdout users, widening the treatment-holdout gap.
A 2% contamination rate over 3 weeks out of 12 months is negligible — the estimate is effectively unbiased.
The direction of the bias is indeterminate without knowing whether the contaminated users were higher or lower value than the average holdout user.
explanation: Option A is correct. Intent-to-treat (ITT) analysis counts contaminated users as holdout — their actual behavior (which includes 3 weeks of feature exposure) partially inflates the holdout arm's revenue. This narrows the treatment-holdout gap, understating the true incremental lift. The direction of the bias is determinate: holdout arm revenue goes up (due to contamination), so the gap shrinks, so lift is understated. Option B reverses the logic: contaminated holdout users inflate the holdout arm, not the treatment arm. Option C is wrong in both direction and magnitude: the 3-week contamination during a mid-experiment period can have lasting behavioral effects (particularly for retention metrics), and 2% of a holdout group is not trivially small when the effect size is 3.8%. Option D incorrectly claims the direction is indeterminate — the contamination direction (holdout users received treatment) uniquely determines the bias direction (holdout revenue up, gap down, lift understated).
hints: If holdout users accidentally received the feature, does the holdout arm's revenue go up or down?
If holdout arm revenue increases, does the treatment-holdout gap grow or shrink?

title: 5% holdout is too small to detect 0.3% long-run lift — what are the options?
scenario_context: Post-hoc power analysis on your 12-month holdout reveals: with 5% holdout (approximately 50,000 users), your minimum detectable effect (MDE) at 80% power is 1.8% lift. Your actual measured lift is +3.8%, so this holdout was adequately powered. However, the business now wants to know if a future holdout could detect a 0.3% lift (the threshold for a 'meaningful' effect on a large annual revenue base). A 0.3% MDE would require approximately 4.2 million users in the holdout arm.
description: What are the trade-offs in designing a holdout that can detect a 0.3% lift?
options: Detecting a 0.3% lift requires ~4.2M holdout users. At 5% holdout, this implies 84M total users — either the platform must be that large or the holdout fraction must increase. Increasing holdout to 15–20% detects smaller effects but imposes a significant cost: holdout users are permanently deprived of shipped improvements, creating ethical and revenue trade-offs. The right framing is: what is the minimum effect size the business cares about, and what holdout cost is acceptable to detect it? Very small MDEs may not be worth the holdout cost.
The solution is to extend the holdout duration to 24 months — doubling the duration roughly halves the MDE, making 0.3% detectable with the same 5% holdout.
Switch from a global holdout to a feature-specific holdout for high-sensitivity metrics — running 5% holdout per feature independently will aggregate to higher effective power across all features.
Use Bayesian inference instead of frequentist power analysis — Bayesian methods do not have an MDE constraint and can detect arbitrarily small effects with enough evidence.
explanation: Option A is correct. It frames the 0.3% MDE question as a business trade-off (cost of holdout deprivation vs. precision of measurement), which is the right lens. The power calculation is real: 4.2M users in holdout is a massive sample requirement, and the ethical cost of withholding improvements from a large permanent holdout is non-trivial. Option B is wrong: doubling duration does not halve the MDE. MDE scales with the inverse square root of sample size, not with duration directly. Doubling duration increases sample size (more observations) but only if the metric is time-averaged rather than point-in-time; for a 12-month cumulative metric, extending to 24 months changes the metric definition, not just the power. Option C confuses feature-level holdouts with the power calculation — running N separate 5% holdouts does not combine their power for a single effect estimate. Option D is a common Bayesian misconception: Bayesian methods still require sufficient data to update the posterior away from the prior; they cannot detect arbitrarily small effects without large samples.
hints: What is the cost of maintaining a large holdout group for users in that group?
Does extending experiment duration double your statistical power?

title: Mobile segment has 12% non-random missing values — what does this mean for HTE analysis?
scenario_context: Your HTE analysis (from the previous question) found a +6.1% lift on desktop but a -1.3% lift on mobile. A data audit reveals that 12% of mobile users have missing values for the primary conversion metric. Investigation shows the missing data is not random: mobile users with older OS versions (iOS 13 and below, Android 8 and below) are 3× more likely to have missing conversion data. These older OS users tend to have lower baseline conversion rates.
description: What is the implication of this non-random missingness for your HTE finding on mobile?
options: The non-random missingness biases the mobile estimate. Older OS users (who systematically miss conversion data) have lower baseline conversion — if they are disproportionately excluded from the mobile analysis, the observed mobile sample overrepresents higher-converting users. The -1.3% mobile lift is computed on a positively selected subsample, not the full mobile population. The true mobile effect could be more negative (if older OS users respond worse to the treatment) or less negative (if they are unaffected), but it is not the -1.3% measured on the observed subsample.

Non-random missingness biases the overall experiment estimate but not the segment-level HTE — since mobile and desktop are analyzed separately, the missingness only affects the mobile segment's precision, not its direction.
Exclude the 12% missing users and report the HTE on the observed mobile subsample with a note that older OS users are underrepresented.
Impute the missing mobile conversion values using the mean conversion rate of the observed mobile users, then rerun the HTE analysis.
explanation: Option A is correct. Missing not at random (MNAR) data causes selection bias in the observed subsample. Older OS users are systematically excluded from the mobile analysis, and they differ from included users in a way that is correlated with both the treatment and the outcome (they have lower baseline conversion). This means the mobile arm's treatment and control groups are not representative of all mobile users — they overrepresent higher-converting users in both arms. The -1.3% estimate is the effect for the 88% observed mobile users, not for mobile users as a whole. Option B is wrong: segment-level analysis is equally subject to selection bias within the segment. Option C (exclude and note) produces the same biased estimate while appearing more rigorous. Option D (mean imputation) imputes the outcome for users whose outcome is structurally missing for device-related reasons — this assumes MCAR (missing completely at random), which the audit has already disproven.
hints: If older OS users are both more likely to be missing AND have lower baseline conversion, what kind of users are left in your mobile sample?
What is MNAR and why does it cause selection bias at the segment level?

title: PM wants 'no mobile harm' claim in press release — can you support it?
scenario_context: Your HTE analysis showed desktop: +6.1%, mobile: -1.3% (95% CI: -4.1% to +1.5%). The PM wants to include in a public press release: 'The new checkout flow improves desktop experience and does not harm mobile users.' The mobile CI spans zero, so the result is not statistically significant at alpha=0.05.
description: Can you support the 'no harm on mobile' claim, and what is the correct statistical reasoning?
options: Do not support the 'no harm' claim as stated. A non-significant result (CI includes zero) means you cannot reject the null of no effect — it does not mean the effect is zero. The mobile CI (-4.1% to +1.5%) is consistent with a real negative effect of up to 4.1%. 'No harm' requires equivalence testing (TOST) with a pre-specified equivalence margin, not simply failing to reach significance. The correct claim, if supported by equivalence testing, would be 'we found no evidence of meaningful harm beyond X%.'
The 'no harm' claim is statistically supported. The CI includes zero, meaning the result is not significant — this is the standard interpretation that the effect is indistinguishable from zero.
Support the claim but reframe it as 'no statistically significant harm' — this is accurate and appropriate for a press release.
Widen the experiment to mobile-only and run 2 more weeks to get a significant result in either direction before the press release.
explanation: Option A is correct. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. A non-significant result (CI includes zero) means the data is consistent with both zero effect and a meaningful negative effect. The mobile CI of (-4.1% to +1.5%) explicitly includes a -4.1% conversion harm as a statistically compatible outcome — that is a real potential harm. 'No harm' as a factual claim requires demonstrating that the effect is practically zero — i.e., falls within a pre-specified equivalence margin using TOST (two one-sided tests). Without equivalence testing, the correct statement is 'we did not detect a statistically significant mobile effect.' Option B commits the classic null-hypothesis-significance testing error of treating failure to reject as accepting the null. Option C's reframe ('no statistically significant harm') is marginally better but still implies the effect is zero to a general audience. Option D extends the experiment for the wrong reason — the goal is to avoid communicating a falsehood, not to run more data until a convenient result appears.
hints: What does 'CI includes zero' tell you vs. 'the effect is zero'?
What statistical procedure tests equivalence rather than superiority?
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Geo-cluster shows +1.2% lift vs user-level +3.8% — which is the right estimate?
scenario_context: Your referral-sharing experiment measured +3.8% lift at the user level (standard A/B). After discovering network-effect contamination (from the previous question), you re-ran the analysis using geo-cluster randomization across 200 cities. The geo-cluster estimate is +1.2% (95% CI: +0.2% to +2.2%). The user-level and geo-cluster estimates differ by 2.6 percentage points.
description: Which estimate is more likely to be the true causal effect of the referral feature, and why?
options: The geo-cluster estimate (+1.2%) is more likely to capture the true causal effect. User-level randomization in a network product violates SUTVA: treatment users sharing referrals reach control users, inflating the control arm's outcomes and widening the apparent treatment-control gap. Geo-cluster randomization reduces this spillover by keeping treatment and control networks geographically separated. The 2.6pp difference is the estimated magnitude of the SUTVA violation — network contamination made the user-level estimate look 3× larger than the true effect.
The user-level estimate (+3.8%) is more reliable because it has more statistical power (individual users as units vs. 200 cities) and a tighter confidence interval.
Neither estimate is trustworthy — the 2.6pp gap between them indicates a fundamental flaw in the experiment design that makes both estimates unusable.
Average the two estimates (+2.5%) to get a balanced view that accounts for both individual-level and network-level effects.
explanation: Option A is correct. The defining problem in network-effect experiments is SUTVA violation: treatment users' actions (sharing referrals) directly affect control users' outcomes (receiving referrals), so the potential outcomes of each unit are not independent. User-level randomization cannot solve this because the interference travels across the assignment boundary. Geo-cluster randomization is the standard solution: by assigning entire geographic communities to treatment or control, within-city network interactions stay within a single arm. The treatment-control gap is measured between cities, where cross-arm spillover is minimized (only border effects remain). The user-level estimate inflates the apparent lift because treatment users are sharing into the control pool, improving control arm retention and compressing the true gap — so the user-level estimate overstates the true causal effect. Option B conflates statistical power with causal identification: high power estimates an inflated quantity precisely. Option C is incorrect: the gap between the two estimates is itself informative (it quantifies the SUTVA violation), not a sign both are broken. Option D averaging is not statistically principled when one estimator is known to be biased.
hints: In a referral experiment, what happens to control users when treatment users share referral links?
Why does geo-cluster randomization reduce SUTVA violations compared to user-level randomization?

title: Expanding referral experiment to international markets with 8% sharing rate — what changes?
scenario_context: Your US referral experiment used geo-cluster randomization across 200 US cities and found +1.2% lift. You are now expanding to 5 international markets (UK, Germany, Brazil, India, Japan). Preliminary data shows sharing rates vary dramatically: UK 12%, Germany 6%, Brazil 18%, India 22%, Japan 3%. In Japan, network density is low enough that the spillover concern motivating geo-cluster randomization may not apply.
description: How should the experiment design change for the international rollout?
options: Design by market spillover risk, not uniformly. In Brazil and India (18–22% sharing rates), network effects are strong and geo-cluster randomization is essential. In Japan (3% sharing rate, low network density), user-level randomization may be acceptable — the spillover contamination is small enough that SUTVA is approximately satisfied, and user-level randomization provides more power. Run separate experiments per market with appropriate designs, then synthesize results using a meta-analytic approach that respects market-level heterogeneity.

Use geo-cluster randomization uniformly across all international markets — consistency in design is more important than local optimization, and it avoids cherry-picking claims about which markets need geo-clustering.
Combine all international markets into a single geo-cluster experiment using city-level randomization — this maximizes total sample size and power for the global estimate.
Use user-level randomization in all markets but apply a post-hoc network correction factor (dividing the estimated lift by the observed sharing rate) to account for spillover in high-sharing markets.
explanation: Option A is correct. The need for geo-cluster randomization is driven by the severity of SUTVA violation, which scales with network density and sharing rate. Japan's 3% sharing rate implies low cross-arm contamination — the expected number of control users reached by a treatment user's referral is small, making SUTVA approximately satisfied. Applying costly geo-cluster randomization uniformly across markets with very different spillover risks sacrifices power without proportional benefit. The meta-analytic synthesis respects that the effect size (and possibly direction) may differ by market — a pooled global estimate may mask meaningful heterogeneity. Option B is overly rigid: design should be driven by the assumption violations that each design is meant to solve, not by aesthetic consistency. Option C's single global geo-cluster experiment pools markets with different market maturities, regulatory environments, and network densities into one estimate, which is likely heterogeneous. Option D's 'network correction factor' is not a valid statistical procedure — it divides a biased estimate by an unrelated scalar, which does not produce an unbiased causal estimate.
hints: What drives the need for geo-cluster randomization vs. user-level randomization?
In a market with 3% sharing rate, how many control users does a typical treatment user's referral reach?

title: PM accepts 2.5% MDE but CFO wants revenue metric instead of conversion — what changes?
scenario_context: After agreeing to a 2.5% MDE (requiring ~640K users per arm) on checkout conversion rate (from the previous question), the CFO intervenes: 'I don't care about conversion rate — I care about revenue per user. Show me the effect in dollars.' Revenue per user in your platform has mean $28, standard deviation $180 (heavily right-skewed: many $0 sessions, occasional $1000+ transactions). Your current enrollment is 400K per arm and still growing.
description: What happens to your sample size requirement when you switch from conversion rate to revenue per user as the primary metric?
options: Sample size requirements increase substantially. For a continuous metric like revenue per user, sample size scales with (variance / effect_size)^2. Revenue per user has a coefficient of variation of 180/28 ≈ 6.4, which is far higher than a binary conversion rate metric. To detect a $0.70 revenue lift (2.5% of $28 mean) at 80% power with alpha=0.05, the required sample is roughly (2 × 1.96 + 0.84)^2 × (180^2 / 0.70^2) ≈ 4.3 million per arm — approximately 7× more than the 640K needed for the conversion rate MDE.
Sample size requirements decrease when switching to a continuous metric like revenue — continuous metrics carry more information per observation than binary conversion, requiring fewer users.
Sample size requirements are unchanged — the 2.5% MDE applies to any metric regardless of its variance, so 640K per arm is still correct.
Revenue per user cannot be used as a primary metric in A/B tests because its right-skewed distribution violates the normality assumption required for t-tests.
explanation: Option A is correct. The sample size formula for continuous metrics is n = 2 × (z_alpha/2 + z_beta)^2 × σ^2 / δ^2, where σ is the metric standard deviation and δ is the effect size in the metric's units. Revenue per user has σ = $180 and δ = $0.70 (2.5% of $28), giving n ≈ 4.3M per arm. This is ~7× higher than the conversion rate requirement because revenue's high variance (driven by the skewed distribution) requires far more observations to average out. Switching to a high-variance continuous metric without recalculating power is a common and costly mistake. Option B inverts the relationship: more information per observation (higher precision) reduces n, but only if variance is low. Revenue's variance is catastrophically high, overwhelming the 'continuous is better than binary' intuition. Option C is wrong: MDE in relative terms (2.5%) produces wildly different absolute effect sizes (and thus different sample requirements) depending on the metric's mean and variance. Option D is a common misconception: t-tests are robust to non-normal distributions at large n (Central Limit Theorem), though log transformation or bootstrap methods may be preferred for highly skewed revenue metrics.

title: 30-day vs 7-day CUPED covariate raises variance reduction from 35% to 52% — is it worth it?
scenario_context: To address the sample size challenge (from the previous question), your data science team proposes CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) using pre-experiment revenue per user as a covariate. A 7-day pre-period covariate reduces variance by 35%, cutting required sample from 4.3M to ~2.8M per arm. A 30-day pre-period covariate reduces variance by 52%, cutting required sample to ~2.1M per arm. The 30-day covariate requires users to have been active for 30 days before the experiment — this excludes 28% of eligible users who are newer.
description: How do you decide between the 7-day and 30-day CUPED covariate?
options: The 30-day covariate's 17pp additional variance reduction (52% vs 35%) must be weighed against the 28% exclusion of newer users. If new users have different treatment response (likely, given they have less purchase history), the 30-day-covariate experiment answers a different question: 'What is the effect for established users?' The 7-day covariate includes all eligible users with lower exclusion, giving a more representative sample at the cost of slightly more variance. The right choice depends on which population the business decision applies to — if the feature affects all users equally, 7-day is preferred for generalizability; if new-user exclusion is acceptable (e.g., the feature targets established users), 30-day is preferred for efficiency.
Always use the longer covariate window — more variance reduction is strictly better and the 28% exclusion is a minor sample size concern that the remaining 72% compensates for.
Always use the shorter covariate window — excluding 28% of users invalidates the experiment regardless of variance reduction gains.
Use both covariates simultaneously in a multiple regression CUPED model — this maximizes variance reduction to above 52% without excluding any users.
explanation: Option A is correct. CUPED efficiency and sample representativeness are in tension, and the right trade-off is determined by the scope of the business question. The 28% exclusion from the 30-day covariate is not merely a sample size issue — it is a representativeness issue. Newer users who are excluded may respond differently to the checkout feature (less price sensitivity, different funnel behavior, less historical data to correlate with the covariate). If the feature is intended for all users, excluding 28% makes the estimate conditional on user tenure, not the general population. Option B treats variance reduction as universally superior to representativeness, ignoring the external validity concern. Option C treats any exclusion as invalidating — this is too absolute; exclusions that are not related to the treatment effect may be acceptable with appropriate scope caveats. Option D contains a statistical error: you cannot use both 7-day and 30-day pre-period data as separate covariates for users without 30 days of history (those users would have missing 30-day values), so the 'no exclusion' claim is false. Additionally, adding a 30-day covariate for only 72% of users introduces missing data complexity.
